docs.text: Overview # CHASE (Contract-based Heterogeneous Analysis and Systems Exploration) is a framework for requirement capture, formalization, and validation for cyber-physical systems. It features a modular and extensible software infrastructure that can support different domain-specific languages, modeling formalisms, and analysis tools. It has been applied to industrial design examples, including the control of aircraft power distribution networks and the arbitration of a mixed-criticality automotive bus. The requirements of the components and of the system are written as assume-guarantee contracts. With them, CHASE: composes the contracts, and checks that the components refine the system; finds the requirements that are in conflict; checks implementations (state machines, RTL, C functions) against the contracts; repairs the constants of a check that fails, and synthesizes controllers; draws all of it as a diagram. The contracts are written in Python, in the specification language of CHASE, in SystemVerilog Assertions, in the clauses of a C file, or by an AI agent through the MCP server. The front ends build the CHASE representation of a design problem, the libraries manipulate systems and contracts, and the back ends translate the problems for the verification and synthesis tools. $> pip install chase-cps from chase_cps import Contract, refines spec = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], assumptions=["G F !req"], guarantees=["G (req -> F grant)"], name="Spec") impl = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], guarantees=["G (req -> X grant)"], name="Impl") print(refines(impl, spec).status) # valid Where to start # Getting started : install CHASE in two commands, and check a first contract. Installation : the optional tools and the sources, module by module. Demos : design problems, from their requirements to a result. MCP server : CHASE for AI agents. CHASE started at the University of Southern California and the University of Verona, and is developed at the University of California, Berkeley. It is open source, under the BSD 3-Clause License: see Contributing and Publications .

docs.text: Contributing # CHASE is open source, under the BSD 3-Clause License, and contributions are welcome: reports of bugs, questions, demos, documentation, and code. The full guide is CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository of CHASE. Reporting a bug or asking a question # Open an issue on chase-cps/chase , with the version ( chase-cps --version ), the back ends found ( chase-cps doctor ), the smallest specification or script that shows the problem, what CHASE answered, and what you expected. A wrong verdict is the most serious kind of bug: please report it even if you are not sure. Proposing a change # For anything larger than a fix, open an issue first, so that we can agree on the design and the names. Make the change on a branch, with tests: for a change to the contract algebra or to a check, a property test that compares it with its definition. Update the documentation and the changelog, and open a pull request. The CI builds and tests CHASE on Ubuntu and macOS, and runs the demos; it must pass. The operations follow their definitions in the literature, and the names are the terms of contract theory. Sending a pull request # Pull requests are sent on GitHub, to the repository of the part that changes, against its default branch: What changes Repository Branch the Python package, the command line, the build chase master the C++ representation and the contract algebra core-library main the printers for the back ends chase-backends main the specification language and its console logics_tool main the domain languages DSL_tool main the MCP server and its skill chase-mcp main the demos demos main the website chase-cps.github.io master Fork the repository on GitHub, and clone your fork (for chase , with --recursive ). Make the change on a new branch, commit it, and push the branch to your fork. Open the pull request from that branch ("Compare & pull request" on GitHub), and give the number of the issue it answers. A change to a C++ module goes to the repository of the module; once it is merged, the submodule is moved in chase (the maintainers do it, or a second pull request to chase does). Repositories # The repositories are those of the table above, in the chase-cps organization on GitHub; chase collects the others as git submodules, with the scripts to build them. The releases are listed in the changelog . The Python packages are chase-cps and chase-mcp on PyPI.

docs.text: Getting started # This page installs CHASE in two commands, checks a first specification from the command line, then writes the same contracts in Python. Other ways to install CHASE (the sources, the optional tools) are on the Installation page. Install # $> pip install chase-cps $> chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license $> chase-cps doctor The first command installs the Python package and the chase-cps command (Linux and macOS, Python 3.10 or later). The checks call the model checker nuXmv, which the second command downloads into ~/.chase ; nuXmv is free for academic and non-commercial use only (see Installation otherwise). chase-cps doctor lists the tools found and how to install the others. A first check # A specification file holds contracts: here a system that answers every request, and two components, a queue that forwards each request and a server that answers it. NAME: first; CONTRACT System: input boolean variable req; output boolean variable grant; Assumptions: G(F(!(req))); Guarantees: G(req -> F(grant)); CONTRACT Queue: input boolean variable req; output boolean variable fwd; Guarantees: G(req -> X(fwd)); CONTRACT Server: input boolean variable fwd; output boolean variable grant; Guarantees: G(fwd -> X(grant)); Saved as first.ltl , it is checked with: $> chase-cps check first.ltl --refines Queue+Server System refines Queue+Server <= System valid 0.03 s The queue and the server, composed, refine the system: together they do what the system must do. chase-cps view first.ltl --check draws the same file as a web page, first.html , with the result on the boxes ( Diagrams ). The command line page has the other checks, and the specification files page the language. The same in Python # The same contracts in Python: their composition, a counterexample, and requirements in conflict. The contracts # A contract has inputs (controlled by the environment), outputs (controlled by the component), assumptions on the environment, and guarantees of the component, written in LTL. from chase_cps import Contract, refines, verify, unsat_core # Every request is eventually granted, if requests stop infinitely often. system = Contract.from_strings( inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], name="System", assumptions=["G F !req"], guarantees=["G (req -> F grant)"]) # A queue that forwards each request, and a server that answers it. queue = Contract.from_strings( inputs=["req"], outputs=["fwd"], name="Queue", guarantees=["G (req -> X fwd)"]) server = Contract.from_strings( inputs=["fwd"], outputs=["grant"], name="Server", guarantees=["G (fwd -> X grant)"]) Composition and refinement # Variables with the same name are connected: the output fwd of the queue is the input of the server. The composition is computed in closed form by the core library ( contract algebra ); the refinement is checked by nuXmv ( contract-based verification ). both = queue.compose(server) print(refines(both, system).status) valid A counterexample # A server that may stop answering for good does not refine the system: lazy = Contract.from_strings( inputs=["fwd"], outputs=["grant"], name="Lazy", guarantees=["G (fwd -> F grant) | F G !grant"]) r = refines(queue.compose(lazy), system) print(r.status, r.failed) print(r.guarantees.trace) invalid guarantees 0: req=True, fwd=False, grant=True 1: req=True, fwd=True, grant=False 2: req=False, fwd=True, grant=False 3: req=False, fwd=True, grant=False <- loop starts The guarantees fail. The request at step 1 is never granted: grant stays false from step 1 on. The lazy server allows it ( F G !grant ), and the system forbids it. A trace is a prefix followed by a loop repeated forever. Another engine of nuXmv may give another trace. Requirements in conflict # bad = Contract.from_strings( inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], name="Bad", guarantees=["G (req -> X grant)", "G !grant", "F req"]) print(verify(bad).status) print(unsat_core(bad).core) unsat CONTRACT Bad_core input req : bool output grant : bool Assumptions: true Guarantees: G (req -> X grant) G !grant F req verify checks that the assumptions and the guarantees can hold together (A ∧ G satisfiable), which implies compatibility and consistency; here the guarantees cannot hold together. unsat_core gives a minimal set of terms that cannot hold together: removing any of them makes the rest satisfiable. Next # The demos : CHASE on aircraft, hardware, C code, drones, and AI agents. The contract algebra , the checks , and GR(1) synthesis . The same operations from a specification file with the command line , or from an AI agent with the MCP server .

docs.text: Installation # The Getting started page installs CHASE in two commands. This page has the rest, by what you want to do: the Python package , with its optional parts; the tools that run the checks ; the sources : all the modules at once, or one by one; AI agents , through the MCP server. The Python package # $> pip install chase-cps The package has the CHASE library (the C++ core library and its Python interface), the parsers of the specification files and of the DSL, the chase-cps command , and the diagrams . Wheels are available for Python 3.10 to 3.15 on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64, glibc 2.28 or later) and macOS 11 or later (arm64 and x86_64). Windows is not supported: use WSL. Two parts are optional, installed with the package: $> pip install "chase-cps[z3,rtl]" z3 (the solver z3) checks the formulas over a bounded number of steps (static contracts, signal temporal logic) and the real variables, and is needed for repair and optimization ( SMT and optimization ). rtl (Yosys, compiled to WebAssembly) reads Verilog and SystemVerilog, for the hardware checks. The tools that run the checks # The checks call external tools, installed apart from the package: nuXmv for the checks of contracts and LTL (refinement, consistency, compatibility, implementation, cores). NuSMV can replace it. slugs for GR(1) realizability and synthesis. ESBMC or CBMC for the C programs . chase-cps install installs them into ~/.chase , and chase-cps doctor lists the tools found, what each is needed for, and how to install the others: $> chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license # Linux x86_64, macOS arm64 $> chase-cps install nusmv # Linux x86_64 $> chase-cps install slugs # needs a C++ compiler, make, and Boost $> chase-cps install esbmc # Linux; on macOS: brew install esbmc $> chase-cps doctor CBMC comes from its packages ( brew install cbmc , apt install cbmc ). gr1c is needed only for the specifications that CHASE writes for it, and is installed from its sources . The tools are looked up in the PATH and in ~/.chase/bin , or given with the environment variables CHASE_NUXMV , CHASE_NUSMV , CHASE_SLUGS , CHASE_ESBMC , and CHASE_CBMC . On macOS, nuXmv needs the libraries of Homebrew ( brew install libxml2 gmp libedit ). On Linux it needs libxml2 and libedit2 , and the C++ library of GCC 13 or later (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 39, or newer). Without nuXmv nuXmv is free for academic and non-commercial use only. Otherwise the checks run with NuSMV (LGPL) instead. NuSMV has no real type: the real variables are then checked with exact regions when they are only compared with constants, and with predicate abstraction otherwise. From the sources # The sources are needed for the console tools logics_tool and dsl_tool , for the C++ library, and to work on CHASE. They need CMake 3.18 or later, a C++17 compiler, Python 3 with its development files, and pybind11: Ubuntu macOS $> sudo apt-get install build-essential cmake git python3-dev pybind11-dev uuid-dev $> brew install cmake pybind11 All the modules at once # The chase repository has every module as a submodule, and a script that builds and installs them in order: $> git clone --recursive https://github.com/chase-cps/chase $> cd chase $> ./install.sh /path/to/install/directory At the end, the script prints the lines to add to the shell configuration: export PATH="/path/to/install/directory/chase/bin:$PATH" export PYTHONPATH="/path/to/install/directory/chase/lib:$PYTHONPATH" The Python modules are built for the interpreter given by the PYTHON environment variable (by default python3 ). In the same repository, pip install . builds and installs the Python package. One module at a time # Each module is a repository of the chase-cps organization, and only the ones a task needs have to be cloned: core-library : the C++ library that represents contracts and computes their algebra, with its Python interface. Every other module needs it. chase-backends : writes the inputs of nuXmv, slugs, and gr1c from the contracts. third_party : the runtime of ANTLR4 (version 4.5.4), used by the two parsers below. logics_tool : reads the specification files and runs the console. DSL_tool : reads the design-pattern language (DSL) of the power systems. For the C++ library alone, core-library is enough; to write the inputs of the tools, add chase-backends; for logics_tool or dsl_tool , add third_party and the tool. All the modules are installed in one directory, given by the variable CHASE_INSTALL_DIR : $> export CHASE_INSTALL_DIR=/absolute/path/to/install/directory core-library comes first; then chase-backends and third_party; then logics_tool and DSL_tool. Each module is built the same way: $> git clone https://github.com/chase-cps/<module> <module> $> cmake -S <module> -B <module>/build -Dpybind11_DIR=<path to pybind11Config.cmake> $> cmake --build <module>/build $> cmake --install <module>/build The modules are built in Release mode; -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug builds them for debugging, and -DPython_EXECUTABLE=<python> chooses the Python interpreter. On macOS with Homebrew, -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$(brew --prefix) finds pybind11 in place of -Dpybind11_DIR . cmake --build core-library/build --target doc writes the documentation of the C++ library with Doxygen. The libraries are installed in CHASE_INSTALL_DIR/chase/lib , the headers in CHASE_INSTALL_DIR/chase/include , the console tools in CHASE_INSTALL_DIR/chase/bin , and ANTLR4 in CHASE_INSTALL_DIR/third_party . AI agents # The MCP server gives the operations of CHASE to an AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other clients). With uv , nothing is installed by hand: $> claude mcp add chase -- uvx chase-mcp or pip install chase-mcp and the command chase-mcp . The agent skill, which tells the agent how to use the tools, and the settings of the other clients are on the MCP server page. The server needs the same tools as the checks ( chase-cps doctor ). An extension for VS Code, which draws the diagrams in the editor, is in preparation.

docs.text: Contract theory # An assume-guarantee contract specifies a component by what it assumes of its environment and what it guarantees in return. The theory of contracts says how such specifications are composed, compared, and divided, independently of the logic in which they are written; CHASE writes them in linear temporal logic. Environment E sets the inputs Contract C = (A, G) Component M sets the outputs inputs x outputs y assumes A of the environment, guarantees G when A holds A component and its environment. The contract assumes A of the behaviors of the environment, and guarantees G for the behaviors of the component when A holds. Contracts and behaviors # A behavior is a sequence of values of the variables, the inputs x and the outputs y. A formula denotes a set of behaviors. A contract C = (A, G) is a pair of such sets: the assumptions A and the guarantees G. Two contracts with the same A and the same A → G (the saturated guarantees) have the same implementations and environments, so CHASE treats them as equal. Notion Holds when Meaning M is an implementation of C (M ⊨ M C) M ∧ A → G in every environment that satisfies A, M satisfies G E is an environment of C (E ⊨ E C) E → A E behaves as the contract assumes C is compatible A is satisfiable C has an environment C is consistent A → G is satisfiable C has an implementation C1 refines C2 (C1 ⪯ C2) A2 → A1 and (A1 → G1) → (A2 → G2) C1 can replace C2: it assumes less and guarantees more Refinement is what makes design by contracts compositional: if C1 refines C2, every implementation of C1 is an implementation of C2, and every environment of C2 is an environment of C1. A component designed for C1 can take the place of one designed for C2, without looking at the rest of the system. Building contracts from contracts # The composition C1 ∥ C2 is the contract of two components placed side by side, with the variables of the same name connected: it guarantees G1 ∧ G2, under the assumptions that the environment meets both A1 and A2, unless the components themselves violate them. If M1 implements C1 and M2 implements C2, then M1 ∥ M2 implements C1 ∥ C2. The other operations answer other design questions: The quotient C / C1: what must the missing component of a system satisfy? The conjunction C1 ∧ C2: what satisfies two specifications at once? The merging C1 • C2: what are two viewpoints of the same component, together? The separation, the implication, and the coimplication are the adjoints of merging, conjunction, and disjunction. Contract algebra gives their definitions and sources. In CHASE # Formulas : the assumptions and the guarantees are formulas of linear temporal logic over Boolean, integer, real, and bit-vector variables, written in Python, in the CHASE specification language, or in SystemVerilog Assertions. Contract algebra : the operations, computed in closed form or keeping the terms of the contracts. Contract-based verification : the notions of the table above, each reduced to the validity or the satisfiability of a formula, which a model checker decides, with counterexamples and cores. For contracts in the GR(1) fragment of LTL, GR(1) synthesis asks whether a component can be synthesized from its contract.

docs.text: Contract algebra # The operations that build a contract from contracts. They hold for any assume-guarantee contracts, and the CHASE core library computes them in closed form, without a solver. In Python they are methods of Contract , and each one returns a new contract. The operations # C1 = (A1, G1) and C2 = (A2, G2) are saturated contracts: G stands for A → G ( contract theory ). Operation Result (A, G) Python composition C1 ∥ C2 ((A1∧A2) ∨ ¬(G1∧G2), G1∧G2) c1.compose(c2) conjunction C1 ∧ C2 (A1∨A2, G1∧G2) c1.conjoin(c2) disjunction C1 ∨ C2 (A1∧A2, G1∨G2) c1.disjoin(c2) merging C1 • C2 (A1∧A2, (G1∧G2) ∨ ¬(A1∧A2)) c1.merge(c2) quotient C1 / C2 (A1∧G2, (G1∧A2) ∨ ¬(A1∧G2)) c1.divide(c2) separation C1 ÷ C2 ((A1∧G2) ∨ ¬(G1∧A2), G1∧A2) c1.separate(c2) implication C1 → C2 ((A2∧¬A1) ∨ (G1∧¬G2), G2 ∨ ¬G1) c1.imply(c2) coimplication (A2 ∨ ¬A1, (G2∧¬G1) ∨ (A1∧¬A2)) c1.coimply(c2) reciprocal C⁻¹ (G, A) c.invert() adding an assumption b·C (b∧A, b → G) c.assume(b) adding a guarantee C·b (b → A, b∧G) c.ensure(b) saturation (A, A → G) c.saturate() simplification the same contract, with simpler formulas c.simplify() The same operations are commands of the console and tools of the MCP server , with the same names. What each one is for # Putting components together Composition : the contract of two components connected together; variables with the same name are connected. Conjunction : one component that meets two specifications at once (the greatest lower bound). Merging : two viewpoints of the same component, such as its function and its timing. Finding a missing part Quotient : the largest contract C of a missing component such that C2 ∥ C refines C1. Any component that refines C completes the design. Separation : the same for merging: the smallest C such that C1 refines C2 • C. Reasoning about specifications Implication C1 → C2: the largest C such that C ∧ C1 refines C2. Disjunction and coimplication : the least upper bound, and its adjoint. Changing one contract Reciprocal : the contract seen from its environment; the inputs become outputs and the outputs inputs. Adding an assumption gives an abstraction of the contract; adding a guarantee gives a refinement of it. Saturation and simplification give an equivalent contract. Example: the contract of a missing component # The system must grant every request; a queue forwards each request as fwd . What must the server between fwd and grant do? from chase_cps import Contract, refines system = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], name="System", assumptions=["G F !req"], guarantees=["G (req -> F grant)"]) queue = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["req"], outputs=["fwd"], name="Queue", guarantees=["G (req -> X fwd)"]) missing = system.divide(queue) # the quotient server = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["fwd"], outputs=["grant"], name="Server", guarantees=["G (fwd -> X grant)"]) lazy = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["fwd"], outputs=["grant"], name="Lazy", guarantees=["G (fwd -> F grant) | F G !grant"]) print(refines(server, missing).status, refines(lazy, missing).status) valid invalid The server that answers each fwd at the next step can fill the gap; the lazy one, which may stop answering, cannot. The two refinement checks are contract-based verification . Composition with discharge # c1.compose(c2, discharge=True) is a simplification of the composition. The closed form puts all the terms of the two contracts into one large formula; with discharge the result keeps each term, and drops the assumptions of one contract that the other one guarantees (Incer, PhD thesis 2022, Algorithm 2): when c1 drives the inputs of c2, and not the reverse, the assumptions of c2 implied by the assumptions and guarantees of c1 are dropped; when the two feed each other, the discharge goes in one direction only, the one that drops more assumptions; then the terms implied by the others are dropped. This variant uses model checking Each drop is decided by an implication check with nuXmv. The result is an abstraction of the composition: a refinement proved on it holds for the composition, one that fails on it may still hold. The Charger demo uses it. Merging and quotient with discharge # c1.merge(c2, discharge=True) and c1.divide(c2, discharge=True) keep the terms too, and here the result is the same contract as the closed form: the merge is (A1 ∧ A2, G1 ∧ G2), whose saturation is the merge; the quotient assumes A1 and the guarantees of c2, and guarantees G1 and the assumptions of c2. The assumptions of c2 implied by A1 are discharged first; when some are left (A2'), each guarantee g of c2 is assumed as A2' → g; then the terms implied by the others are dropped. The closed forms are rarely GR(1), the terms often are: use these before is_realizable and synthesize . The AHB demo merges two viewpoints, and the BufferSwap demo divides the system by the neighbours of a buffer. Conjunction, disjunction, and separation have no such form: their assumption or guarantee is a disjunction. Quotient: Incer, Benveniste, Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, Seshia, MEMOCODE 2018, Theorem 3.5. Merging and separation: Passerone, Incer, Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, ACM TECS 2019, Theorem 3.12. docs.text: Contract-based verification # The verification tasks on contracts ask whether one contract refines another, whether a contract can be met at all, and whether a component or an environment satisfies a contract. They are defined on behaviors, for any assume-guarantee contracts. CHASE carries them out for contracts in LTL over Boolean, bounded integer, real, and word variables: each task reduces to the validity or the satisfiability of a formula, which a model checker decides ( back ends ). Verification tasks # Task Holds when Python refinement C1 ⪯ C2 A2 → A1 and (A1→G1) → (A2→G2) are valid refines(c1, c2) compatibility some environment satisfies A is_compatible(c) consistency some behavior satisfies A → G is_consistent(c) assumptions and guarantees together A ∧ G is satisfiable (so compatible and consistent) verify(c) implementation M ⊨ M C M ∧ A → G is valid, or every behavior of the state machine M satisfies A → G is_implementation(m, c) environment E ⊨ E C E → A is valid, or every behavior of E satisfies A is_environment(e, c) receptiveness of a state machine M M refuses no input that the assumptions allow is_receptive(m, c) no redundant terms each term is not implied by the others remove_redundant(c) M and E are LTL formulas over the variables of the contract. A failed check comes with a counterexample: a behavior that breaks it. remove_redundant(c) drops the terms implied by the others, keeping A → G; before synthesis, use remove_redundant(c, synth=True) ( GR(1) synthesis ). With core=True , each removed term comes with the terms that imply it. r = refines(impl, spec) r.status # "valid" or "invalid" r.failed # "assumptions" or "guarantees", when invalid r.guarantees.trace Queries on formulas # The checks above are built on two queries, which can also be called directly: Query Question Answer implies(phi, psi, variables) validity : does phi → psi hold for every behavior? valid , or invalid with a behavior that satisfies phi and violates psi is_satisfiable(phi, variables) satisfiability : does some behavior satisfy phi? sat with such a behavior, or unsat A formula is satisfiable; a component satisfies a contract is_satisfiable asks whether some behavior (a value of each variable at each step) satisfies a formula. Whether a component satisfies a contract is is_implementation(m, c) . docs.text: Formulas # The assumptions and the guarantees of a contract are formulas of linear temporal logic (LTL) over variables of four types. The Python package, the command line (JSON files), and the MCP server read them in the standard LTL syntax described here; the specification files of logics_tool use the logics language , with the same operators and the same precedence. Assertions written in SystemVerilog are read as the same formulas (see SystemVerilog Assertions below). Variables # Type Written Values Boolean "bool" true, false Integer range [0, 3] (in the logics language integer (0:3) ) the integers from 0 to 3 Real "real" any real number Word "word[8]" , "signed word[8]" a bit vector of 8 bits, unsigned (0 to 255) or in two's complement (-128 to 127) The inputs are controlled by the environment, the outputs by the component. Names start with a letter and are not keywords ( G , F , X , U , R , W , P , NAME , CONTRACT , mod , xor , ...). from chase_cps import Contract counter = Contract.from_dict({"name": "Counter", "inputs": {"inc": "bool", "step": [1, 3]}, "outputs": {"n": "word[8]", "k": [0, 9]}, "assumptions": ["G F inc"], "guarantees": ["G (inc -> n' = n + 1)", "G (k <= 9 - step -> k' = k + step)"]}) tank = Contract.from_dict({"name": "Tank", "inputs": {"flow": "real"}, "outputs": {"level": "real"}, "assumptions": ["G (0 <= flow & flow <= 1.5)"], "guarantees": ["G (level' = level + 0.5 * flow)"]}) Logic # Operators Meaning ! , & , \| , -> , <-> , xor , true , false the Boolean connectives X p p holds at the next step G p , F p p holds at every step, at some step p U q , p R q , p W q until, release, weak until G[a,b] p , F[a,b] p , p U[a,b] q the same over the steps a to b x' the value of x at the next step past(x, n) the value of x n steps before (any value in the first n steps) The aliases are: [] and <> for G and F ; && , || , => , <=> , and == for & , | , -> , <-> , and = . The temporal operators apply to formulas. Inside a relation or an arithmetic expression, the value at the next step is written x' , not X x . For instance, G X X (y = past(x, 2)) says that y is x delayed by two steps; past is written under X , so that it never reads before the first step. Relations and arithmetic # The relations = != < <= > >= compare two expressions of the same type; a Boolean is compared only with = and != . Type Operators Notes Integer + - * / mod the values stay in the range of the variables; a constant compared with an integer should be in its range Real + - * / constants with a fraction ( 20.5 ) are read exactly; linear arithmetic is decided exactly, nonlinear may not finish Word + - * / mod modulo 2^n: for a word[8] equal to 255, x + 1 = 0 Word & \| xor ! bitwise; in a relation, parenthesize them: (x & y) = 0 Word << >> shifts by a number ( >> keeps the sign of a signed word) Word x :: y concatenation, x on the high bits Word x[7:4] , x[3] bits; a single bit can be used as a Boolean Word extend(x, n) , signed(x) , unsigned(x) n more bits; the same bits read as signed or unsigned Both operands of an operation on words have the same width and signedness, and an integer constant takes the type of the other operand: x + 1 with x : word[8] is a word[8] . A word does not go with an integer variable; make both words. A formula that does not type is refused when the contract is built, with the reason. Precedence # From the loosest to the tightest: <-> , -> , | xor , & , U R W , the unary operators ( ! G F X ), the relations, << >> , + - , * / mod , :: , the bits x[7:0] . -> and U R W group to the right, the other binary operators to the left. So G a -> b is (G a) -> b ; write G (a -> b) . This is the precedence of LTL tools such as Spot, NuSMV, and nuXmv, and of the logics language. What takes which formulas # Checks (nuXmv) Contract algebra GR(1) synthesis (slugs) Logics language Booleans, integers yes yes yes, in the GR(1) fragment yes Reals yes yes real variables compared with constants yes Words yes yes no no past(x, n) yes yes no no The checks are exact for Booleans, integers, and words. Repair # When a check fails, repair finds the values of named constants (a deadline, a threshold, a bound) that make it pass, at the least cost, and changes nothing else. Each constant is given a range; the cost is by default the change, the sum of |p - p0|, or any term with minimize or maximize . from chase_cps import Contract, repair impl = Contract.from_strings(name="Impl", inputs={"x": (0, 9)}, outputs={"y": (0, 20)}, guarantees=["y = x + 5"]) spec = Contract.from_strings(name="Spec", inputs={"x": (0, 9)}, outputs={"y": (0, 20)}, guarantees=["y <= x + lam"], constants={"lam": 4}) r = repair("refines", impl, spec, parameters={"lam": (0, 10)}) print(r.status, r.values, r.optimal) # repaired {'lam': 5} True flowchart TD A["A check fails: refines, impl, env, verify, ..."] --> B["The constants that may change,
their ranges, and a cost"] B --> C{"Which formulas?"} C -->|"G and F of one step"| D["copies: the state written n+1 times,
no temporal operator"] C -->|"a bounded number of steps"| E["projection: the values that fail,
at once (z3)"] C -->|"some behavior:
verify, compat, consist"| W["witnesses or enumeration"] C -->|"LTL, C code, the rest"| F["the least cost that avoids
the counterexamples found so far (z3)"] D --> O["the least cost (z3)"] E --> O W --> O O --> K["the check itself, with the values"] F --> G{"the check with these values
(nuXmv, ESBMC)"} G -->|"a new counterexample"| F K --> R(["repaired: the values, their cost, optimal"]) G -->|"passes"| R O -->|"no values"| I(["impossible"]) F -->|"no values"| I G -->|"time limit"| U(["unknown"]) How a repair goes. The method is chosen by the formulas, and the values found always pass the check itself. The answer is repaired (the values, their cost, and whether it is the least), holds (the present values already pass), impossible (no values in the ranges pass), or unknown with the reason. The methods: copies (from 0.6.4): terms that are G or F of one step. A counterexample needs only one state per term, so the question is written on that many copies of the state, with no temporal operator, and solved exactly (Demri and Schnoebelen, Information and Computation 2002, Proposition 7.2). projection : formulas over a bounded number of steps; the values that fail are computed at once. counterexamples : the rest (LTL, C code). Each counterexample rules out the values it breaks; the cost of each round is a lower bound, so the first values that pass are the least. With several real constants it may not end: give time_limit . witnesses and enumeration : checks that some behavior exists ( verify , compat , consist ). On the command line, --param NAME=LOW..HIGH ( :int for an integer): $> chase-cps repair heater.ltl --refines Room+Thermostat Comfort --param theta=60..90:int repair repaired (counterexamples, 5 rounds, 0.13 s) theta = 74 change 2 (optimal) In a diagram , a click on a red tag opens the same repair, and Apply writes the values into the file; the checks that read them run again. The demos Drone timing , Room thermostat , Resource arbiter , and Drone climb repair a timing bound, a thermostat and its C code, a deadline in LTL, and two constants at once.

When a check fails, repair finds the values of named constants (a deadline, a threshold, a bound) that make it pass, at the least cost, and changes nothing else. Each constant is given a range; the cost is by default the change, the sum of |p - p0|, or any term with minimize or maximize . from chase_cps import Contract, repair impl = Contract.from_strings(name="Impl", inputs={"x": (0, 9)}, outputs={"y": (0, 20)}, guarantees=["y = x + 5"]) spec = Contract.from_strings(name="Spec", inputs={"x": (0, 9)}, outputs={"y": (0, 20)}, guarantees=["y <= x + lam"], constants={"lam": 4}) r = repair("refines", impl, spec, parameters={"lam": (0, 10)}) print(r.status, r.values, r.optimal) # repaired {'lam': 5} True flowchart TD A["A check fails: refines, impl, env, verify, ..."] --> B["The constants that may change,
their ranges, and a cost"] B --> C{"Which formulas?"} C -->|"G and F of one step"| D["copies: the state written n+1 times,
no temporal operator"] C -->|"a bounded number of steps"| E["projection: the values that fail,
at once (z3)"] C -->|"some behavior:
verify, compat, consist"| W["witnesses or enumeration"] C -->|"LTL, C code, the rest"| F["the least cost that avoids
the counterexamples found so far (z3)"] D --> O["the least cost (z3)"] E --> O W --> O O --> K["the check itself, with the values"] F --> G{"the check with these values
(nuXmv, ESBMC)"} G -->|"a new counterexample"| F K --> R(["repaired: the values, their cost, optimal"]) G -->|"passes"| R O -->|"no values"| I(["impossible"]) F -->|"no values"| I G -->|"time limit"| U(["unknown"]) How a repair goes. The method is chosen by the formulas, and the values found always pass the check itself. The answer is repaired (the values, their cost, and whether it is the least), holds (the present values already pass), impossible (no values in the ranges pass), or unknown with the reason. The methods: copies (from 0.6.4): terms that are G or F of one step. A counterexample needs only one state per term, so the question is written on that many copies of the state, with no temporal operator, and solved exactly (Demri and Schnoebelen, Information and Computation 2002, Proposition 7.2). projection : formulas over a bounded number of steps; the values that fail are computed at once. counterexamples : the rest (LTL, C code). Each counterexample rules out the values it breaks; the cost of each round is a lower bound, so the first values that pass are the least. With several real constants it may not end: give time_limit . witnesses and enumeration : checks that some behavior exists ( verify , compat , consist ). On the command line, --param NAME=LOW..HIGH ( :int for an integer): $> chase-cps repair heater.ltl --refines Room+Thermostat Comfort --param theta=60..90:int repair repaired (counterexamples, 5 rounds, 0.13 s) theta = 74 change 2 (optimal) In a diagram , a click on a red tag opens the same repair, and Apply writes the values into the file; the checks that read them run again. The demos Drone timing , Room thermostat , Resource arbiter , and Drone climb repair a timing bound, a thermostat and its C code, a deadline in LTL, and two constants at once.

docs.text: AMBA AHB bus arbiter: two viewpoints that cannot be merged, and the assumption that fixes them # The system. AMBA AHB is the on-chip bus of ARM processors. Several masters (processors, DMA engines) share it, and an arbiter decides which one has the bus. This demo has two masters, simplified from Bloem et al., "Specify, Compile, Run: Hardware from PSL" (COCV 2007). A master asks for the bus ( hbusreq1 , hbusreq2 ) and may ask for a locked access ( hlock1 , hlock2 ): a series of transfers that nobody may interrupt. The arbiter gives the bus ( hgrant1 , hgrant2 ) and says when it is locked ( hmastlock ). Two teams wrote two viewpoints of the arbiter in SystemVerilog Assertions: Grant (the bus goes to exactly one master, to master 1 at the start, and no master waits forever) and Lock (a master that has locked the bus keeps it while it asks for it). Merging (•) puts two viewpoints of one component together: the arbiter must meet both. slugs checks realizability and synthesizes controllers; nuXmv checks the controller. The question. Is there an arbiter that meets both viewpoints, and if not, what must it assume of the masters? Each team's viewpoint can be fine on its own while the two together ask for the impossible, and this is best found before the arbiter is built. The system: the arbiter, the merge of the two viewpoints. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. Each viewpoint. A contract is realizable when some controller meets it whatever the masters do. Grant and Lock are each realizable. Step 2. The merge, without the last assumption of Lock. Without G F !(hmastlock & ((hgrant1 & hbusreq1) | (hgrant2 & hbusreq2))) , the merge is unrealizable. CHASE finds the unrealizable core , 5 of its 7 guarantees: when master 1 locks the bus and keeps asking for it, Lock lets it keep the bus ( G ((hmastlock & hgrant1) -> X (hbusreq1 -> hgrant1)) ), and Grant says that master 2 does not wait forever ( G F (hbusreq2 -> hgrant2) ). The initial grant, the single grant, and the lock rule complete the core. Step 2: the merge without the assumption is unrealizable; the terms of the core are red. Step 3. What the arbiter must assume. The core points at the missing assumption: a master that has locked the bus stops asking for it sooner or later (the third assumption of Lock , LA2 in the paper). With it, the merge Arbiter is realizable, and slugs synthesizes a controller of 81 states. Arbiter is also written as SVA in out/arbiter.sv , for a tool that checks an arbiter written by hand. Step 3: Arbiter, the merge with the assumption, is realizable. Step 4. The controller. The synthesized controller, read as a state machine, implements Arbiter (M ⊨ C). Step 4: the controller implements Arbiter (M ⊨ C). Run it # pip install chase-cps chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license chase-cps install slugs python ahb.py --expect The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.

docs.text: Aircraft power system: the bounds as written conflict, relaxed they are realizable # The system. The electric power system of an aircraft, from Nuzzo et al., "CHASE: Contract-based requirement engineering for cyber-physical system design" (DATE 2018). A left and a right generator each feed an AC bus, a rectifier, a DC bus, and a load. Contactors (switches) connect each generator to its AC bus (contactors 1 and 2), and the two AC buses to each other (contactor 3). A controller opens and closes the contactors; it reads the state of the generators and of the contactors, and commands the contactors. The system and its requirements are written in the language of CHASE for power systems (read by load_dsl ), which turns them into a GR(1) contract for the controller (GR(1) is the fragment of LTL that a synthesis tool such as slugs solves): it assumes that a contactor switches in 10 ms or less and that at most one generator fails, and guarantees, among others, that the generators never run in parallel and that no DC bus stays without power more than 15 ms. Times become counters: a step is 5 ms. The question. Can the contactors be switched so that the requirements hold whatever fails? If not, which requirements are in conflict? The answer tells the system engineers which bound to renegotiate before anyone designs the controller. The system: the controller of the contactors, with its inputs and outputs. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. The requirements as written. The contract (11 inputs, 7 outputs, 30 assumptions, 28 guarantees) is not realizable : no controller meets it whatever the generators do. CHASE finds the unrealizable core , 4 of the 28 guarantees: contactors 1, 2, and 3 are never all closed, and the three terms of the counter of one DC bus allow it at most 15 ms without power. When a generator fails, its DC bus can be fed again only through contactor 3, after the contactor of that generator opens: two switchings of up to 10 ms each, more than 15 ms. Step 1: the requirements as written are unrealizable; the terms of the core are red. Step 2. The relaxed requirements. template_0_realizable.txt changes two lines: 20 ms to disconnect a failed generator, 30 ms for a DC bus (a step is then 10 ms). The contract (24 assumptions, 26 guarantees) is realizable, and slugs synthesizes a controller of 97 states from it. Step 2: the relaxed requirements are realizable (R). The same language describes a factory . Run it # pip install chase-cps chase-cps install slugs python eps.py --expect sh solution.sh /tmp/eps runs both versions with dsl_tool and slugs. The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.

docs.text: Circuit buffer swap: the new buffer fails the old contract, but the quotient shows it fits # The system. In a circuit, a producer sends data to a consumer through a buffer, with a ready/valid handshake: the producer offers a value ( v_i ) and keeps it until the buffer is ready ( ready_o ); the buffer offers a value to the consumer ( v_o , data_o ) until the consumer takes it ( yumi_i ). The buffer is bsg_two_fifo , a FIFO of two entries from BaseJump STL , an open library of hardware blocks in SystemVerilog. The requirement of the whole, Pipeline , says that every offer is taken sooner or later, and that an offered value stays until it is taken. Each part has a contract written in SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA); Yosys reads the Verilog of the buffers into state machines, and nuXmv checks them. The question. The designer wants to replace the buffer with bsg_one_fifo , a FIFO of one entry, which is smaller. Its contract does not refine the old one. Can it still take the place of the old buffer, and what must any buffer in that place satisfy? Answering from the contracts avoids checking the whole circuit again for every candidate. The system: the producer, the buffer, and the consumer, inside the requirement Pipeline. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. The old system. Producer , TwoFifo , and Consumer , composed, refine Pipeline , and the Verilog of bsg_two_fifo implements TwoFifo (M ⊨ C). Step 1: the old system refines Pipeline; the Verilog implements TwoFifo. Step 2. The new buffer against the old one. OneFifo does not refine TwoFifo , so it cannot replace it on the strength of its contract alone. In the counterexample of 4 steps, the empty buffer takes a value at step 1 and is not ready at step 2, where TwoFifo guarantees that it is. Step 2: OneFifo does not refine TwoFifo; the guarantee it breaks in red. Step 3. What the place needs. CHASE computes the quotient Slot = Pipeline / (Producer ⊗ Consumer), the dashed box: the weakest contract any buffer in that place must meet, derived from the contracts. It has 3 assumptions and 3 guarantees. Slot may assume what the consumer guarantees, that an offer is taken sooner or later ( G (v_o -> F yumi_i) ), so one entry is enough: OneFifo refines Slot , and the system with OneFifo refines Pipeline . Step 3: OneFifo refines Slot, the contract of the place. Step 4. On the Verilog. The Verilog of bsg_one_fifo implements OneFifo and Slot , and does not implement TwoFifo . The script also writes Slot as SVA ( out/slot.sv ), so that a commercial tool such as Jasper can check any new buffer against it ( jasper/run.tcl , not run by the script). Step 4: the Verilog of bsg_one_fifo implements its contract (M ⊨ C). Run it # pip install "chase-cps[rtl]" # with Yosys chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license python bufferswap.py --expect The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.

docs.text: Robot charging station: refinement does not see the conflict, realizability does # The system. Two robots share one charging station, and an arbiter decides who charges. This is a teaching example, made for these pages; its requirements are numbered in requirements.txt . Robot i asks for the station ( req_i ) when its battery is low ( low_i ), and assumes that it gets it ( grant_i ), or stops asking, infinitely often. The arbiter reads the requests and sets the grants; it must never give the station to both robots, G !(grant1 & grant2) . The contracts are in LTL over Booleans, in the GR(1) form of the synthesis tool slugs, so CHASE can ask whether a controller can be built from a contract (realizable) and build it. ChargingStation is the contract of the whole system. The question. Five candidate arbiters are written: Greedy , Fair , Pushy , Polite , and Trusting . Four of them are flawed in a different way. Which check catches which flaw, and which arbiter works with the robots? The system: an arbiter (here Fair) between the two robots, inside ChargingStation. The steps # Step 1. Greedy: unrealizable, yet it refines. Greedy grants each request at the next step, G (req1 -> X grant1) and the same for robot 2. When both robots ask at once it cannot serve both without breaking G !(grant1 & grant2) : it is unrealizable, no arbiter can do it. The unrealizable core, the smallest set of guarantees in conflict, is these three formulas. Yet Greedy with the robots refines ChargingStation : refinement only compares formulas (every behavior allowed by the parts is allowed by the system) and does not ask whether a part can exist. Step 1: the core of Greedy in red. Step 2. Fair: realizable. Fair gives the station to each robot, or the robot stops asking, infinitely often, G F (grant1 | !req1) and the same for robot 2. It is realizable, and slugs builds a controller of 18 states. It is not vacuous: it cannot meet its guarantees without setting its outputs (¬V). remove_redundant removes its last guarantee, G F (grant1 | !req1 | grant2) , implied by the first one. Step 2: Fair is realizable (R) and not vacuous (¬V). Step 3. Realizable for a bad reason. Pushy assumes that robot 1 asks infinitely often, G F req1 , but never right after a grant, G (grant1 -> X !req1) . By granting robot 1 at every step, the arbiter makes the robot break the first assumption, and then owes nothing. A contract is well separated (WS) when the component cannot win this way; Pushy is not, and the core is the two assumptions. Polite , which assumes G ((req1 & grant1) -> X !req1) instead, is well separated. Step 3: Pushy is not well separated; Polite is. Step 4. An arbiter that never grants. Trusting is Fair with two more assumptions, G F !req1 and G F !req2 : each robot stops asking infinitely often. Its guarantees then hold with no grant at all: it is vacuous. docs.text: Contracts in C: each function checked against the clauses in its file # The system. Small C functions of controllers: the pump of a water tank ( tank.c ), a ring buffer ( ring.c ), and a limit on the climb rate of a drone ( climb.c ). Their contracts are written in the C file itself, as the C checkers ESBMC, CBMC, and Frama-C read them: requires clauses say what a call may assume (the assumptions of the contract), ensures clauses what the function must give back (its guarantees). CHASE reads these clauses, in any of the three syntaxes, and draws each function as a component whose inputs are its parameters and whose output is its return value. ESBMC (or CBMC) checks one call of the function against its contract. The clauses CHASE reads are listed on the page C programs . The question. Does each function meet the contract written next to it, and what does a failure look like? Code with no contract at all: can it at least be checked for overflow? The same file then serves the C checker and the contracts of a whole system. The system of tank.c : pump , with the terms read from its clauses, and flow , with none. The steps # Step 1. The pump meets its contract. pump (clauses of ESBMC) runs at full speed (3) from a level of 80 and is off below 20. ESBMC proves that every call within the assumed levels, 0 to 100, gives back what the contract asks, in about 0.1 s (the tag M ⊨ C). Step 1: pump meets the contract read from its clauses. Step 2. Code with no clause. flow divides the liters by the seconds. With no contract, it is checked for overflow, division by zero, and failed asserts (the tag safe ). liters / seconds overflows for liters = -2147483648 , seconds = -1 ; the panel gives the line. Step 2: flow is not safe code. Step 3. The ring buffer, with and without the wrap. advance (clauses of CBMC) gives the next slot of a ring buffer of 8 slots, and meets its contract. advance_fast does not wrap at the end: the slot i = 7 gives ni = 8 , and the term ni <= 7 is red. The failing call is on the ports, ready to replay. Step 3: advance meets its contract, advance_fast does not. Step 4. A contract in ACSL. climb.c limits the climb rate of the drone of the page Drone climb to 3, with its contract in an ACSL comment, /*@ ... */ , the language of Frama-C. limit meets it (ESBMC checks it; Frama-C is not run). limit_loose tests the top with v > 4 , so v = 4 gives 4. Step 4: limit meets its ACSL contract, limit_loose does not. docs.text: Resource arbiter: the least bound on a waiting time # The system. An arbiter shares a resource, such as a bus or a memory port, among clients. Here there is one client and an arbiter on a fixed schedule. Client raises req and holds it until it gets grant . Arbiter has a counter c that goes 0, 1, 2, 0, ..., and grants when c = 2 . Wait is not part of the hardware: it only counts in w how many steps the current request has waited, so that the requirement can speak of it. The requirement, MaxWait , is G (w <= k) : no request waits more than k steps, with the named constant k set to 1 in deadline.ltl . The formulas are LTL over runs that never end, and the model checker nuXmv checks them. The question. What is the least k the arbiter can promise? The designer of a client needs this number to set its timeouts: too small, and a correct arbiter is rejected; too large, and the promise is of little use. The system: the client, the arbiter, and the counter of the wait, inside the requirement. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. The bound is too small. Client , Arbiter , and Wait , composed, do not refine MaxWait with k = 1 . nuXmv gives a run that loops forever: a request made at c = 0 is granted at c = 2 , after 2 steps ( w = 2 ), and the run goes back to step 0. Step 1: w reaches 2 at step 2, when the grant comes. Step 2. Repair the bound. repair finds k = 2 and shows that no smaller value works. Each round looks for the least k under the condition that the counterexamples found so far are no longer counterexamples (the one of step 1, with w = 2 , gives k >= 2 ), then checks that k with nuXmv. Two rounds: k = 1 fails, k = 2 passes. Each condition only removes values that cannot work, so the value that passes is the least. Checking each k from 0 to 9 gives the same answer with ten runs of nuXmv; the repair needs two, and works the same on real numbers, where there is nothing to enumerate. Step 2: Find repairs, k picked: 1 to 2, optimal. A second question: the arbiter and the client as state machines # Arbiter assumes that a request is held until it is granted. Does an arbiter written as a state machine meet its contract, and does it accept every request the client may send? arbiter.smv writes the arbiter in SMV, the language of nuXmv, with req as an input ( IVAR ): it implements Arbiter (M ⊨ C) and is receptive, that is, it takes every request the assumption allows. refusing.smv adds the constraint TRANS c = 0 -> !req : it still implements Arbiter , but only because it refuses a request after c = 2 , and the check of receptiveness says so. On the other side, client.smv is an environment of Arbiter (E ⊨ A: it meets the assumption); impatient.smv , which may stop asking before the grant, is not: its counterexample asks at step 0 and stops at step 1. The arbiter as a state machine, and the two clients. Run it # pip install "chase-cps[z3]" chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license python deadline.py --expect chase-cps view deadline.ltl --check --serve chase-cps check deadline.ltl --recep refusing.smv Arbiter --env impatient.smv Arbiter The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.

docs.text: Drone climb: no controller beats the wind # The system. A drone of a fire-suppression mission climbs to the altitude where it drops its water, r = 20 m. The fire makes a vertical wind w (up or down, at most wmax per step) that pushes the drone. The drone comes from the mission of ContrACT (Xiao, Lutz, Castillo-Effen, Nuzzo, MEMOCODE 2026). Drone starts on the ground at height h = 0 and moves by v + w each step. Climb , the controller, sets the climb rate v to half the error to r , at most vmax (3 m per step). The requirement Hover : while the wind stays within wmax , the drone is within eps (2 m) of r for 5 steps, starting at one of the first 10, and is never above r + eps . The contracts are in signal temporal logic in discrete time, checked by z3. The question. Does the drone get there in time and stay long enough? If not, should the controller change, or the requirement? A faster controller costs a stronger motor; a looser requirement costs water dropped from farther away. The system: the drone and its controller inside the requirement Hover. The steps # Step 1. The wind decides. Drone and Climb composed refine Hover (every behavior of the two meets it) in a wind of 0.5 m per step, not of 1. The robustness of Hover , the margin by which it holds in the worst case, is 0.75 m in a wind of 0.5. In a wind of 1 it is -0.5 m: in the counterexample the wind always pushes down, and the drone is at 17.5 m at step 10, the last step where the 5 steps can start, 0.5 m below the band of 18 to 22 m. Step 1: a counterexample in a wind of 1, step 7 on the ports. Step 2. The controller cannot fix it. repair looks for values of named constants that make the check pass at the least change. For vmax it finds none, and proves it: near the target, with the wind down, the error goes as e' = e/2 + 1 , so it stays above 2 m however fast the drone climbs. Step 2: vmax picked, its range widened to [0, 9]: no value works. Step 3. The requirement. The least tolerance is eps = 2.5 m (2.49 fails): the 0.5 m of step 1. Or, keeping eps = 2 , the strongest wind is wmax = 17/21 , about 0.81 m per step (0.82 fails). Step 3: eps 2 to 2.5, or wmax 1 to about 0.8095 (17/21). Step 4. Both at once. With two constants free, a cost says which change is worse: (eps - 2) + w (1 - wmax) , a change of the wind counting w times a change of the tolerance. With w = 2 the repair lowers the wind to 17/21 (cost 8/21); with w = 3 it widens the tolerance to 2.5 (cost 1/2). Each answer is the least cost over every mix of the two changes, which is hard to find by trying values. r = repair("refines", drone, hover, parameters={"eps": (2, 10), "wmax": (0, 1)}, minimize="(eps - 2) + 3 * (1 - wmax)") The tags of the pictures are explained on the page Diagrams . docs.text: Fire-suppression drones in C: a collision found and fixed on the contracts, then checked one function at a time # The system. Two drones of a fire-suppression mission move on a 10 x 10 grid, one cell per step. They come from the multi-drone fire suppression of ContrACT (Xiao et al., MEMOCODE 2026), whose software is written as reactions, pieces of code run at each step. Each step has five parts, each with a contract and a C function: Plan0 and Plan1 ( plan.c ): each drone at (x, y) asks for a move r toward its target (tx, ty) : 0 stay, 1 right, 2 left, 3 down, 4 up; Coordinator ( coordinator.c , function grant ): grants the moves g , refusing two moves into the same cell or a swap; Move0 and Move1 ( move.c ): each drone moves as granted, to (nx, ny) . The requirement Fleet : two drones in different cells are, after the step, in different cells, and do not cross. The contracts are on integers, checked by z3; the C functions by ESBMC. The question. Can two drones end in the same cell? And can each C function be checked alone, without checking the whole program? A whole program check grows with every function; one function at a time does not. The system: one step of the two drones inside the requirement Fleet; each part has its C function. The steps # Step 1. The contracts do not refine the requirement. The five parts composed do not refine Fleet (some behavior of the parts breaks it). In the counterexample, drone 0 is at its target (1, 0) and stays, and drone 1 at (2, 0) moves left into its cell: the coordinator compares only drones that both move. The script finds the same failure for a swap. Step 1: the parts with Coordinator do not refine Fleet . Step 2. The fix. No number can be tuned: the rule must change. CHASE computes the quotient of Fleet by the other four parts: the weakest contract the coordinator must meet so that the step meets Fleet (see the contract algebra ). Coordinator does not refine it. CoordinatorSafe , which grants a move only into a cell that is free after the step, does, and the parts with it refine Fleet . Step 2: the parts with CoordinatorSafe refine Fleet . Step 3. The code. ESBMC checks each function against its contract (the tag M ⊨ C), in about 0.1 s each. The five functions of the step ( plan0 , plan1 , grant , move0 , move1 ) implement theirs. grant does not implement CoordinatorSafe ; grant_safe does. With steps 2 and 3, the C code with grant_safe keeps the drones apart, and the whole program is never checked at once. Step 3: grant_safe implements CoordinatorSafe . The tags of the pictures are explained on the page Diagrams . docs.text: Drone timing: the bound, a faster timer, and its repair # The system. Three drones put out fires on a grid, coordinated over a network. The software is written in Lingua Franca, where each component runs reactions (pieces of code triggered by an event). This is the multi-drone fire suppression of ContrACT (Xiao, Lutz, Castillo-Effen, Nuzzo, MEMOCODE 2026), with the worst-case times of each reaction of its Table III. Each event v has three times: its timestamp t_v (when it is due, on the logical clock), its start d_v , and its completion T_v . In the pictures, T_c3 is the completion of the planner and d_s3 - t_s3 the delay of the move of a drone. docs.text: OpenTitan security chip: the escalation link proven module by module from its RTL # The system. OpenTitan is an open source security chip. When it detects an attack, an alert handler sends an escalation (an order to react, for instance to wipe the keys) to a receiver, over an escalation link. This demo is a small version of that link: Sender , Channel (the wires), and Receiver , each a Verilog module. To escalate, the sender raises a differential pair: two wires with opposite values ( esc_p_tx , esc_n_tx ), so a single wrong wire makes them equal, which both ends detect. To ping (test that the receiver is alive), it sends one-cycle pulses; a pulse of two cycles is an escalation. The inputs err_ep , err_en , err_rp , err_rn flip one wire of the channel, to model a fault or an attack. The contracts of the modules and the two requirements are written in SystemVerilog Assertions, after the assertions of OpenTitan ( prim_esc_rxtx_assert_fpv ): Functional (with no wrong wire, a request held two cycles escalates the receiver, nothing else does, and a ping is answered) and Integrity (a single wrong wire is detected). Yosys reads the Verilog into state machines, and nuXmv checks them. The question. Does the link meet both requirements, and can we show it by checking each module on its own? Checking modules one by one scales to designs too large to check at once, and a module can then be replaced by any other that meets its contract. The system: the three modules, each with its Verilog, inside the requirement Functional. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. Each module. The Verilog of the sender, of the channel, and of the receiver implements its contract (M ⊨ C: every behavior of the module meets the contract). The receiver is drawn open: its contract and its state machine of 4 states, read from the Verilog. Step 1: the receiver implements its contract (M ⊨ C); its state machine of four states. Step 2. The link. The contracts of the three modules, composed, refine Functional and Integrity . With step 1, this proves that the link meets both requirements, without a check of the whole design. Checked as a whole, the Verilog of the link meets both too, as it should. Step 2: each module implements its contract, and the link refines Functional. Step 3. A faster sender. A sender that pings at every cycle of a ping request does not implement Sender . In the counterexample, the ping request stays high and so does the pair, which only an escalation may do. The module check finds the fault in the sender alone; in the whole link, the same sender makes the receiver escalate on a ping. Step 3: the fast sender does not implement Sender; the guarantee it breaks in red. docs.text: Room thermostat: repairing the threshold, then checking its C code # The system. A thermostat keeps a room warm without overheating it. It is a small example made for these pages. Room starts at 60 degrees and, at each step, gains the heat u and loses 1. Thermostat heats ( u = 3 ) while the temperature T is below a threshold theta , here 76; it is also written in C, in heater.c . The requirement Comfort asks T <= tmax (75 degrees) at every step. The contracts are written in signal temporal logic in discrete time over 10 steps ( G[0,10] is "at each of the steps 0 to 10"), so the solver z3 checks them. The question. Does the thermostat keep the room within 75 degrees? If not, which threshold does, and does the C code implement it? The designer needs a threshold that works before tuning the code. The system: Room and Thermostat (with its C code) inside the requirement Comfort. The steps # Step 1. The thermostat overshoots. Room and Thermostat composed do not refine Comfort (refine: every behavior of the parts meets the requirement). The counterexample: the room heats to 76, cools to 75, and heats again to 77 at step 10. CHASE also computes the robustness of T <= 75 , the margin by which it holds in the worst case: -2, two degrees too hot. Steps 1 and 2: the counterexample at the top (the slider puts step 8 on the ports), the two repairs at the bottom. Step 2. Repair. repair changes a named constant as little as possible so that the check passes, and shows that no smaller change works. On the thermostat it gives theta = 74 , a change of 2: the room then reaches 75 and no more. On the requirement it gives tmax = 77 : the requirement accepts the overshoot. In the viewer, tmax belongs to the requirement and is picked only by hand. Step 3. The code. Each step of Thermostat is one call of the C function, so ESBMC checks one call against one step of the formula (the tag M ⊨ C). With theta = 76 it fails: the call with T = 75 returns 0 where the contract asks for 3. repair finds the threshold that the code implements: 74. Step 3: M ⊨ C fails on T = 75. Step 4. Between the samples. A step is a sample taken every 20 s, and the temperature changes at most 0.1 degree per second (its Lipschitz constant: a bound on how fast it changes). Between two samples it can then move by 2 degrees, so CHASE checks T + 2 < 75 at the samples (Fainekos and Pappas): if that holds, T <= 75 holds at every instant. With theta = 74 the samples reach 75: the answer is unknown, not a counterexample, since the margin is only sufficient. With theta = 71 the refinement holds in continuous time. $> chase-cps check heater.ltl --period 20 --lipschitz T=0.1 --refines Room+Thermostat Comfort The tags of the pictures are explained on the page Diagrams . Run it # pip install "chase-cps[z3]" # and ESBMC or CBMC for step 4 python heater.py --expect chase-cps view heater.ltl --check --serve The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.

docs.text: NASA Lift-Plus-Cruise aircraft: what the pilot must do to hover in time # The system. Lift-Plus-Cruise is a NASA concept of an electric aircraft that takes off and hovers on lift rotors and cruises on a wing. Its mode logic sets lift_mode : 3 wing borne (flying on the wing), 2 semi wing borne, 1 semi thrust borne, 0 thrust borne (hovering on the rotors). It reads the airspeed kias and the ground speed kgs (knots), and the hover control hover_control_mode , which the pilot turns on. The requirements come from the LPC_mini example of FRET , the requirements tool of NASA (Pressburger et al., REFSQ 2023), as LTL formulas over real numbers, one formula per requirement. The vehicle is split in two parts: ModeLogic , with the requirements on the modes, and Pilot , which sets the speeds and the hover control: it starts at 120 knots and changes the speed by at most 10 per step. The checks run on nuXmv, with its SMT engine for the reals. The question. The requirements say what the mode logic does, not what the pilot does, so some flights hover within 12 steps and others never do. What must the pilot do so that every flight hovers in time? A designer of the pilot, or of a flight procedure, needs exactly this contract. The system: the pilot drives the mode logic, inside the requirements with the deadline of 12 steps. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. Two deadlines. With a deadline of 12 steps the requirements are consistent: some flight meets them all. With 6 they are not, and CHASE finds the unsat core , the smallest set of requirements in conflict: 8 of 18. They say why: kias starts at 120 and changes by at most 10 per step, the vehicle stays wing borne above 90 and semi wing borne above 30, so it cannot hover by step 6. Step 1: consistent with 12 steps, not with 6; the core in red. Step 2. The split. ModeLogic ⊗ Pilot (their composition) refines Vehicle , the requirements without a deadline. Step 2: the split refines the vehicle. Step 3. What the pilot must do. CHASE computes the quotient Q12 = Reach12 / ModeLogic, the dashed box: the weakest contract of the pilot with which every flight hovers within 12 steps. It is derived from the requirements, not written by hand. Pilot , with the requirements alone, does not refine it: in the counterexample kias stays at 120 and the vehicle never leaves the wing. Step 3: Pilot does not refine Q12: kias stays at 120. Step 4. A pilot that slows down. Slow lowers kias by 10 per step, but never turns the hover control on: the vehicle stops at semi thrust borne, and Slow does not refine Q12. Step 4: Slow slows down, but never turns the hover control on. Step 5. A pilot that turns on the hover control. Decel also turns the hover control on when kgs is below 20, and refines Q12: with the mode logic, every flight hovers within 12 steps. It does not refine Q06 = Reach06 / ModeLogic: no pilot can, as step 1 showed. Step 5: Decel refines Q12. Step 5: Decel does not refine Q06: at step 6 the vehicle is still semi wing borne. docs.text: Lockheed Martin autopilot: the requirements in conflict, and the time the pullup takes # The system. An autopilot of an aircraft commands a safety maneuver, a pullup, when a sensor reports that the flight limits are exceeded. The requirements come from the Ten Lockheed Martin Cyber-Physical Challenges (Mavridou et al., RE 2020), first as written and then corrected, as in the case study LMCPS of FRET , the requirements tool of NASA. Each requirement is a transition of a state machine, written in LTL ( x' is x at the next step). Autopilot has the states STATE 0 TRANSITION, 1 NOMINAL, 2 MANEUVER (the pullup), 3 STANDBY; it reads standby (the pilot is in control), apfail (an external failure), supported (the system is healthy), and good (the sensor sees no fault). Sensor has the states SENSTATE 0 NOMINAL, 1 TRANSITION, 2 FAULT; it reads limits (the limits are exceeded) and the mode of the autopilot. The contracts assume nothing of the environment. slugs checks realizability, nuXmv the refinements. The question. Two questions. Which of the first requirements are in conflict, so that no autopilot can meet them? And once they are corrected, does the pullup come as soon as the system requirement says? The first is asked before anyone builds the autopilot, the second before anyone signs off its timing. The system: the autopilot and the sensor, inside the system requirement, FSM-001. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. The first requirements. A contract is realizable when some state machine meets it whatever the environment does. The first requirements of the autopilot are not. CHASE finds an unrealizable core , the smallest set of requirements that no machine meets together: the initial state, G ((STATE = 0 & standby') -> STATE' = 3) , and G ((STATE = 0 & supported' & good) -> STATE' = 1) . In TRANSITION, with the pilot in control and good data, one says STANDBY and the other NOMINAL. The script replaces one requirement per core by its corrected version until the contract is realizable: four conflicts in the autopilot, one in the sensor, the ones FRET reports. Finding them by reading 14 requirements is hard; each core points at two to four. Step 1: the first requirements; the cores in red. Step 2. The system. The corrected Autopilot and Sensor are realizable. Composed, they do not refine Pullup , G ((limits & !standby & !apfail & supported) -> pullup) : a pullup at the step the limits are exceeded. In the counterexample, the limits are exceeded at step 1, but the autopilot is still in NOMINAL. Step 2: the composition does not refine Pullup; the values at step 1. Step 3. The system, with time. The sensor and the autopilot each take a step to react. PullupTimed gives the pullup that time: after three steps within the limits and one beyond, with the pilot not in control and no failure, the pullup comes at the fifth step. The composition refines it. Step 3: the composition refines PullupTimed. Run it # pip install chase-cps chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license chase-cps install slugs python fsm.py --expect The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.

docs.text: Payment assistant agent: the plan of an AI agent checked before it runs # The system. An AI agent gets a task from a user and splits it among sub-agents, each holding some of the tools. The task comes from AppWorld , a benchmark of agents that use phone apps: pay Kristin back on Venmo the amount in her text messages, with the note "Groceries", then text her "It is done.", and send no voice message. Each variable is a tool call or what it writes: tx2 (a payment made by sub-agent 2), paid (the payment is done), text3 (a text sent by sub-agent 3), desc_ok and msg_ok (the note and the text are the ones asked for), voice1 , voice3 (voice messages), complete (the task marked done). The contract of the parent, Parent , is the request and the rules of the user, written in LTL; it assumes nothing. The sub-agents are Messages (finds the amount), Payment (pays), Text (sends the text), and Keep , what the parent keeps for itself (marking the task complete). Each sub-agent gets a contract from the tools it holds. nuXmv checks the contracts. The question. Do the contracts of the sub-agents, together, give the contract of the parent? If not, what must a sub-agent promise? The answer is known before any tool is called, so a plan with a gap is fixed before it pays anyone. The plan: the four sub-agents inside the contract of the parent. The steps # The tags on the boxes give the results of the checks: green holds, red fails; Diagrams says how to read them. Step 1. The plan does not refine the parent. The plan refines the parent (⪯) when every behavior of the sub-agents together meets the contract of the parent. It does not: no sub-agent promises F text3 (the text is sent, sooner or later). nuXmv gives a run that pays and never sends the text. Step 1: the plan does not refine the parent; in the counterexample text3 stays false. Step 2. What sub-agent 3 must do. CHASE computes the quotient Q3 = Parent / (Messages ⊗ Payment ⊗ Keep): the weakest contract that the missing sub-agent must meet so that the plan refines the parent. It is derived from the contracts, not written by hand. Q3 asks for the rules of the tools of sub-agent 3 and F text3 . Text , with F text3 added, refines Q3 (it is drawn in Q3, the dashed box), so the plan refines the parent. Step 2: Text, with F text3 and the assumption F paid , refines Q3. Step 3. A rule against the request. If the parent also says "never pay" ( G !tx2 , in ParentWithSlip ), no behavior meets its contract: it is inconsistent. CHASE finds the unsat core , the smallest set of guarantees in conflict: F tx2 and G !tx2 , two of nine. Step 3: the inconsistent parent, with the core in red. docs.text: Pick-and-place arm: the mission refines the target, and the coordinator is synthesized # The system. A robotic arm picks a piece, turns, and places it at a target position. The example is the second part of a tutorial at the DATE 2021 University Booth; the first part is the aircraft power system . specs/robotic_arm.ltl has seven contracts in LTL over Booleans and small integers: Target , the requirement: request a pick ( rpick ) until the piece is picked, then a place ( rplace ); Mission , the design of the mission planner: the same requests, and also the target position ( xtarget , ytarget ) and the angle ( desired_angle ) for each phase; Coordinator : commands the pick and the place ( cmd_pick , cmd_place ) once the arm is in position and turned; Move , Turn , Pick , Place : the four actions of the arm, which report pdone , adone , picked , placed . nuXmv checks the contracts and slugs synthesizes controllers. The steps use the console of logics_tool , the command-line tool of CHASE. The question. Does the mission meet the requirement? Do the seven contracts fit together, that is, can their assumptions and guarantees all hold? And can the coordinator be built from its contract? These are the checks to run before writing any code for the arm. flowchart LR Mission -- "rpick, rplace" --> Coordinator Mission -- "xtarget, ytarget" --> Move Mission -- "desired_angle" --> Turn Move -- pdone --> Coordinator Turn -- adone --> Coordinator Coordinator -- cmd_pick --> Pick Coordinator -- cmd_place --> Place Pick -- "picked, grip" --> Coordinator Place -- placed --> Coordinator Pick -- picked --> Mission Place -- placed --> Mission The system: the mission planner, the coordinator, and the four actions, with the signals between them. The steps # Step 1. The mission refines the target. Mission refines Target : it assumes no more and guarantees at least as much, for every behavior. The console runs the commands of solution.script and writes the checks for nuXmv, which finds both formulas true: $> logics_tool -i specs/robotic_arm.ltl -o /tmp/ -c solution.script $> nuXmv /tmp/MT.smv Step 1: Mission refines Target (⪯ green). Step 2. The other direction. The reverse check shows that Mission says more than Target , so the design is a true refinement and not a copy of the requirement: Target does not refine Mission . In /tmp/TM.smv the formula of the guarantees is false. In the counterexample the piece is picked at step 1, and at step 2 xtarget , ytarget , and desired_angle are still 0: Target says nothing about them. Step 2: Target does not refine Mission; the counterexample at step 2. Step 3. The whole system. compose builds the system of the seven contracts, and verify writes the negation of its assumptions, of its guarantees, and of both. nuXmv -bmc /tmp/system.smv finds a run for each: the system is compatible (some environment meets its assumptions) and consistent (the parts can meet their guarantees). Step 4. The coordinator. synthesize Coordinator coordinator slugs writes the coordinator for slugs, which finds it realizable (a controller exists for every behavior of the arm and the mission) and synthesizes one of 128 states. By hand this controller would be written and then tested; here it comes from its contract. The tags of the pictures are explained on the page Diagrams . Run it # pip install chase-cps chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license chase-cps install slugs sh diagram.sh The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.
