docs.text: Robotic arm joints: checked and synthesized one joint at a time # The system. A robotic arm with three joints moves each joint to the angle it is asked for. The example was shown at CPS-IoT Week 2022 ( CPSWeek22 has the original files). Joint i reads a request req_ji , the angle asked for ji_dangle , and its present angle ji_angle (0 to 4); it writes a command ji_cmd (0 stay, 1 up, 2 down) and ji_done . Its contract assumes that a request is held until the joint is done and that the angle follows the command; it guarantees that the joint is done exactly at the angle asked for, and done infinitely often ( G F ji_done ). Joints , the contract of the arm, has the assumptions and the guarantees of the three joints. The contracts are LTL over bounded integers, checked by nuXmv; the controllers are built by slugs. The question. Do the three joint contracts, composed, meet the contract of the arm? Can a controller be built for each joint alone, rather than one for the arm? And how does the check grow with the number of joints? An arm maker wants to add joints without redoing the proof. The system: the three joints inside the contract of the arm; Joint1 open (the others are the same with 2 and 3). The steps # Step 1. The joints refine the arm. The composition of the three joints refines Joints : it assumes no more and guarantees at least as much, for every behavior. verification.chase writes this check for nuXmv in refinement.smv , and nuXmv proves both formulas. diagram.sh draws the same check: every tag is green, the composition refines (⪯), and each joint's assumptions and guarantees can hold together (A∧G) and it is realizable (R). Step 1: Joint1 and Joints open: what one joint and the arm assume and guarantee. Step 2. One controller per joint, not one for the arm. synthesis.chase writes one file for slugs per joint, and slugs builds a controller of 72 states for each. singlemodel.chase writes Joints alone: it is realizable too, but its controller has at least 375,000 states, about 72 x 72 x 72, and slugs does not finish writing it. With step 1, the three small controllers are enough: their composition meets the contract of the arm. Step 3. Scaling. scaling.py builds the same contracts for N joints and checks the refinement: about 1 s for 3 joints and 5 s for 8 (Apple M4 Pro, nuXmv 2.2.0). With --broken , Joint1 does not guarantee G F j1_done , and nuXmv finds a counterexample of 3 or 4 steps for every N. The tags of the pictures are explained on the page Diagrams . Run it # pip install chase-cps chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license chase-cps install slugs python scaling.py --joints 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 --broken --expect compositional_demo.sh and singlemodel_demo.sh run steps 1 and 2 with the console. The files of the demo are in the repository ; Running the demos says what the scripts print and how to use the diagrams.

docs.text: Running the demos # Each demo is a directory of the demos repository. Its page ends with the commands that run it. Install # The Python package and the back ends that a demo uses: $> pip install chase-cps $> chase-cps install nuxmv --accept-license $> chase-cps install slugs nuXmv checks refinement, compatibility, and consistency; slugs checks realizability and synthesizes controllers (GR(1)); pip install "chase-cps[z3]" adds z3, for the contracts over real numbers and for repair; pip install "chase-cps[rtl]" adds Yosys, which reads the RTL; ESBMC or CBMC checks the C programs. The scripts # Each demo has a Python script, named after the demo. The script prints the result of each step, with the counterexamples, and writes the diagrams of the demo in out/ . With --expect , the script also compares each result with the one on the page, and exits with code 1 when one differs. $> python heater.py --expect Some demos also have a diagram.sh , which writes the same diagrams with the command line ( chase-cps view ). The diagrams # The pages in out/ open in a browser. On a diagram: a box is a contract or a component; a box inside another refines it; the tags next to a name are its checks: green holds, red does not; a click on a red tag opens the panel with the counterexample; the slider steps through it, and the values appear on the ports; the wrench at the top opens and closes the panel; it lists the checks that fail; Esc closes the help, then the panel. docs.text: Interfaces # The operations of CHASE have the same names in every interface. Here is one contract, an arbiter that grants every request when the requests stop infinitely often, and the check that an implementation that grants at the next step refines it, in each interface: Python, the CHASE specification language (Spec), the command line (CLI), SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), and the MCP server for AI agents (MCP). Python Spec CLI SVA MCP from chase_cps import Contract, refines spec = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], assumptions=["G F !req"], guarantees=["G (req -> F grant)"], name="Spec") impl = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], guarantees=["G (req -> X grant)"], name="Impl") print(refines(impl, spec).status) # valid NAME: arbiter; CONTRACT Spec: input boolean variable req; output boolean variable grant; Assumptions: G(F(!req)); Guarantees: G(req -> F(grant)); CONTRACT Impl: input boolean variable req; output boolean variable grant; Assumptions: true; Guarantees: G(req -> X(grant)); $> chase-cps check arbiter.ltl --refines Impl Spec refines Impl <= Spec valid 0.03 s module spec (input logic clk, input logic req, output logic grant); A1: assume property (@(posedge clk) s_eventually !req); G1: assert property (@(posedge clk) req |-> s_eventually grant); endmodule parse_sva reads this module as the contract Spec: the ports give the inputs and the outputs, assume the assumptions, and assert the guarantees. {"tool": "refines", "arguments": { "refined": { "name": "Impl", "inputs": {"req": "bool"}, "outputs": {"grant": "bool"}, "guarantees": ["G (req -> X grant)"]}, "abstract": { "name": "Spec", "inputs": {"req": "bool"}, "outputs": {"grant": "bool"}, "assumptions": ["G F !req"], "guarantees": ["G (req -> F grant)"]}}} The interfaces are: Python package : for scripts and notebooks ( pip install chase-cps ). Command line : to check or draw a specification file ( chase-cps check , chase-cps view ). Specification language and console : the .ltl files of CHASE, and the console of logics_tool. SystemVerilog Assertions : contracts read from SVA, and written back as SVA. MCP server for AI agents : the operations as tools of an agent, with a skill that tells the agent how to use them. Diagrams : contracts, components, and systems drawn as a web page, with the results of the checks. Model checking, GR(1) synthesis, and the tools that read SystemVerilog are described in Tool integrations .

docs.text: Command line # The Python package installs the chase-cps command, with the commands check , repair , view , export , install , and doctor . In the options, a contract is NAME , or NAME+NAME+... for the composition of the contracts. A model is a state machine in an SMV file, or in a JSON file (a state machine, or a controller of slugs synthesized from the contract). Checking a specification # chase-cps check checks the contracts of a specification file in the logics language of CHASE, or of a JSON file (one contract, a list of contracts, or {"contracts": [...]} , each in the format of Contract.from_dict ), and prints the counterexamples. Usage chase-cps check FILE [options] Parameters: Contract-based verification (nuXmv): --verify The assumptions and the guarantees can hold together (A ∧ G satisfiable). It is the default when no check is given. --compatible Some environment satisfies the assumptions. --consistent Some behavior satisfies A → G. --contracts C... The contracts checked by the three options above (default: all). --refines R A R refines A. It may be repeated. --implementation MODEL C The model is an implementation of C. --environment MODEL C The behaviors of the model satisfy the assumptions of C. --receptive MODEL C The model accepts every input that the assumptions of C allow. GR(1) synthesis (slugs): --realizable C C is realizable. It may be repeated. --synthesize C Synthesizes a controller for C. It may be repeated. --well-separated C The component cannot win by forcing the environment to violate its assumptions. --vacuous C The component can win without an output that a liveness guarantee asks for. For every check: --core When a check fails, gives a minimal set of terms that explains it. --json Prints the results as JSON. --timeout S Seconds for each check. --backend auto|nuxmv|nusmv The model checker. --engine auto|ic3|bdd|bmc|portfolio The engine of the model checker. Continuous time (a step is a sample): --period S The time between two steps. The intervals may then be written with times: G[0s,2s] , F[0ms,500ms] . --lipschitz VAR=RATE... How fast each variable changes, per second (or one RATE for every variable). --refines then holds in continuous time, between the samples too ( sampled signals ). For instance: $> chase-cps check specs.ltl # verify every contract $> chase-cps check specs.ltl --refines Joint1+Joint2 Joints # the composition refines Joints $> chase-cps check specs.ltl --realizable Joint1 --json $> chase-cps check specs.ltl --implementation joint1.smv Joint1 --receptive joint1.smv Joint1 $> chase-cps check plant.ltl --period 0.1 --lipschitz x=2 --refines Plant Req The exit status is 0 when every check passes, 1 when a check fails or does not finish, and 2 on an error in the input. Drawing a specification # chase-cps view writes the diagram of a file as a web page. The file is a specification in the logics language, in JSON, or in SystemVerilog Assertions ( .sv ), or a Verilog module ( .v , or .sv without assertions), drawn with its state machine. Usage chase-cps view FILE [options] Parameters: What is drawn: --contracts C... The contracts drawn. By default, all the contracts of the file, but those drawn inside another box. --refines R A Draws R inside A. It may be repeated. --implementation MODEL C Draws C as a component with its model: SMV, JSON, or RTL read with Yosys ( FILE:MODULE for a file with several modules). It may be repeated. --environment MODEL C Draws the model as an environment of C, on its left. It may be repeated. --open C... Draws these contracts open: their terms, and the core of a check that fails. The checks: --check Checks that the assumptions and the guarantees of each contract can hold together (A∧G, with the core when they cannot), and the refinements, the implementations, and the environments drawn (nuXmv or NuSMV). --verify Checks that each contract drawn is compatible and consistent. --realizable Checks that each contract drawn is realizable (slugs); when it is not, marks the guarantees of the core. --timeout S Seconds for each check. --budget S No check starts after S seconds; the checks left are not marked. --results FILE Where the results of --check are kept (default: next to the file, charger.ltl → charger.results.json ). A check of contracts that have not changed is read from it, not run again. --no-results Keeps no results. --no-checks Leaves the three checks above out. The page: -o PAGE The page written (default: FILE with .html ). --format html|json The page, or the data of the diagram. --elk PATH Puts a local elk.bundled.js in the page, which then works offline (default: ELK from a CDN). --serve Serves the page on this computer, and draws it again whenever the file changes. When the file cannot be drawn, the page keeps the last diagram and says why. The repairs of the page run there, and Apply writes the values into the file ( Diagrams ). --host HOST , --port PORT Where the page is served. For instance: $> chase-cps view specs.ltl # writes specs.html $> chase-cps view specs.ltl --refines Joint1+Joint2+Joint3 Joints --check --realizable $> chase-cps view specs.ltl --open Joints --serve # drawn again on each change $> chase-cps view arbiter.v # the module and its states Without --refines and --contracts , the contracts are put together by their ports: an output and an input with the same name are wired; contracts with the same inputs and outputs are versions of one part (fixes, or candidates): the first one in the file is wired, the others are drawn apart; a contract whose outputs are driven by several parts, which read from outside only its inputs, is the contract of their composition: the parts are drawn inside it, and --check checks the refinement; when two parts or more are written but some outputs of the contract are driven by none, the part not written yet is drawn as a hole: the quotient of the contract by the parts. The options can also be written at the top of the file, in comments ( // view: in Verilog). The files named there are taken from the folder of the file: # view: --implementation models/arb.json Arb --check --open Arb CONTRACT Arb ... Repairing and exporting # chase-cps repair FILE takes the checks of chase-cps check and --param NAME=LOW..HIGH ( :int for an integer), and finds the values of the constants that make the check pass ( Repair ). chase-cps export FILE --to smv|smt|gr1|sva|c|spec|json writes a check, or the contracts, as the input of a tool you run yourself: nuXmv or NuSMV ( smv ), z3 or cvc5 ( smt ), slugs or gr1c ( gr1 ), an SVA checker, ESBMC or CBMC ( c ). docs.text: Diagrams # CHASE draws contracts, components, and systems as a web page, with the results of the checks on the boxes. The page opens in a browser and works offline with a local copy of ELK, the layout library. A quotient, drawn as a dashed box, with the part that refines it inside ( Payment assistant agent ). What is drawn # Boxes C a contract M a component with a model: RTL read with Yosys, a state machine in JSON or SMV, or a controller synthesized by slugs; a model with few states opens on its state graph E an environment, on the left of what it drives ? a quotient: the missing part, with the part checked against it inside a box inside another is checked against it, on as many levels as there are refinements; the ⪯ tag says whether it refines it C A req G ack an open contract: its assumptions (A) and its guarantees (G); ⊤ when it has none C C1 ⊗ C2 how the contract is built: ⊗ composition, ∧ conjunction, • merging (viewpoints of one component), / quotient Buttons on a box show the assumptions and the guarantees show the composed contract (⊗) show the model given (RTL, JSON, SMV) show the model synthesized (slugs) fold what is inside the box Results of the checks: green when the check holds, red when it does not refinement A A compatible G G consistent A∧G A∧G feasible R R realizable WS WS well separated ¬V ¬V not vacuous M ⊨ C M ⊨ C the model implements the contract E ⊨ A E ⊨ A the environment meets the assumptions G !g1 the core of a failed check, shown by a click on a red tag Wires a Boolean an integer or a real 8 a bus, with its width req an input that nobody drives: its name in orange, after a dashed stub A term of a specification file shows its line when the pointer rests on it. Drag to move the diagram, and use the wheel (or a pinch) to zoom; the key 0 fits it to the window. A box keeps its row when a box is opened. The button with an arrow saves the whole diagram as SVG, PNG, or PDF. A check that fails # A click on a red tag opens a panel beside the diagram. The panel lists every check that fails (Problems), and for the one chosen (Details): the counterexample, step by step, opened at the step where a term first fails; a slider puts the values of a step on the wires, and the terms that the step breaks turn red in the boxes. Find repairs gives the values at the least cost ( Repair ); Preview draws them on the diagram, and Apply writes them into the file. The checks that read the constant run again, and the diagram shows whether another check still fails. The repairs run on the page served by chase-cps view FILE --serve . Python # from chase_cps import Component, Contract, System, refines, viz a = Contract.from_strings(name="A", inputs=["x"], outputs=["y"], guarantees=["G (x -> X y)"]) b = Contract.from_strings(name="B", inputs=["y"], outputs=["z"], guarantees=["G (y -> z)"]) top = Contract.from_strings(name="Top", inputs=["x"], outputs=["y", "z"], guarantees=["G (x -> X z)"]) s = System("S", [Component("a", a), Component("b", b)], contract=top) s.check() # the composition against Top q = top.divide(a, name="Q") # what the part next to a must do refines(b, q) # the result is kept on b d = viz.diagram(s, q, refines=[(b, q)], open=[q]) viz.save(d, "plan.html") # viz.show(d) opens a browser The options of viz.diagram : refines lists the pairs (R, A) where R is drawn inside A. environments lists the environments, each with what it drives. open lists the boxes drawn open when the page loads. checks lists results of checks to draw. In Jupyter, a system or a contract draws itself. Command line, MCP, and VS Code # Command line: chase-cps view FILE draws a specification file, or a Verilog module. The contracts are put together by their ports: the outputs and inputs of the same name are wired, and the parts whose composition has the ports of another contract are drawn inside it; a part not written yet is drawn as a hole, the quotient. docs.text: Specification language and console # This page is for writing contracts in a file rather than in Python: the language of the .ltl files, which the command line, the Python package, and the diagrams read, and the console logics_tool , built from the sources. Specification files # The specification files ( .ltl ) are written in the logics language of CHASE. They are read by the console, by chase_cps.load_spec , and by chase-cps check . NAME: arbiter; CONTRACT Spec: input boolean variable req; output boolean variable grant; input integer (0:3) variable n; Assumptions: G(F(!(req))); Guarantees: G(req -> F(grant)); NAME: name; names the system; CONTRACT name: starts a contract. Variables: input or output , boolean , integer (low:high) , or real , then variable name; . An integer without a range ranges over 0 to 16; load_spec and parse_spec warn when an integer is compared with a constant outside its range, since the comparison then has the same value at every step. Declarations outside the contracts are shared: each contract gets those it uses. A real is declared without a range (the Python package rejects real (low:high) : write the range as an assumption). Constants are declared as integer constant N 5; or real constant K 2.5; , and propositions as proposition p is x > 3; . Assumptions: and Guarantees: list formulas, each ending with ; . Formulas: ! (or ~ ), & (or /\ ), | (or \/ ), -> , <-> , G , F , X , U , R , P(...) (probability), true , false , the relations = != < <= > >= , the arithmetic + - * / , and x' for the value of x in the next step. # starts a comment. The precedence is that of the formulas : G a -> b is (G a) -> b ; write G (a -> b) . The console of logics_tool # logics_tool reads a specification file and runs commands, interactively or from a script: $> logics_tool -i specs.ltl -o out/ -c script.chase The commands are: the operations of the contract algebra , with their names: compose C1 C2 R , conjoin C1 C2 R , divide C1 C2 R , ...; saturate C , simplify C , and show C ; verify C file and refines C1 C2 file , which write an SMV model; synthesize C file solver , which writes a specification for slugs or gr1c. The variables of two contracts are matched: by name (the default); by a map entered by hand ( manual as last argument); by a map read from a file (its name as last argument). The console writes the input files of the external tools, which are run by hand. The Python package, the command line, and the MCP server run the tools and return the result. When the SMV file has real variables or real numbers, the console says so: NuSMV cannot read it, and nuXmv checks it with its SMT engine: $> nuXmv -int refinement.smv nuXmv > go_msat nuXmv > check_ltlspec_ic3

docs.text: logics_tool reads a specification file and runs commands, interactively or from a script: $> logics_tool -i specs.ltl -o out/ -c script.chase The commands are: the operations of the contract algebra , with their names: compose C1 C2 R , conjoin C1 C2 R , divide C1 C2 R , ...; saturate C , simplify C , and show C ; verify C file and refines C1 C2 file , which write an SMV model; synthesize C file solver , which writes a specification for slugs or gr1c. The variables of two contracts are matched: by name (the default); by a map entered by hand ( manual as last argument); by a map read from a file (its name as last argument). The console writes the input files of the external tools, which are run by hand. The Python package, the command line, and the MCP server run the tools and return the result. When the SMV file has real variables or real numbers, the console says so: NuSMV cannot read it, and nuXmv checks it with its SMT engine: $> nuXmv -int refinement.smv nuXmv > go_msat nuXmv > check_ltlspec_ic3

docs.text: MCP server for AI agents # chase-mcp is a Model Context Protocol server that gives the operations of CHASE to AI agents as tools. With them, an agent writes assume-guarantee contracts, composes them, checks refinement, and uses the counterexamples and the cores to fix the specification. A skill tells the agent how to use the tools. Tools # The tools have the names of the Python package. They are grouped as follows: Contract algebra : compose , conjoin , disjoin , merge , divide , separate , imply , coimply , invert , assume , ensure , saturate , simplify . Contract-based verification : refines , verify , is_compatible , is_consistent , is_implementation , is_environment , is_receptive , remove_redundant . refines takes period and lipschitz to check a refinement in continuous time. Repair : repair , the values of named constants that make a check pass. Queries on formulas : implies , is_satisfiable , unsat_core . GR(1) synthesis : is_realizable , synthesize , unrealizable_core , is_well_separated , is_vacuous , and remove_redundant with synth . Formats : parse_spec and to_spec (specification files), parse_sva and to_sva (SystemVerilog Assertions), rtl_ports (the ports of RTL read with Yosys; RTL is given to is_implementation and the other checks of state machines), parse_smv (an SMV model with its LTLSPEC and INVARSPEC ). C programs : parse_c (the contracts written in a C file: clauses of ESBMC, CBMC, or ACSL) and check_c (each function against its own contract, with ESBMC or CBMC). Diagrams : visualize . It tells the agent: how to turn requirements into contracts: the variables and who controls them, and one pattern for each requirement; which group each tool belongs to; how to report a result in the words of the requirements: which requirement fails and when, and which parts of an answer hold for every behavior and which come from one counterexample. docs.text: Python package # chase_cps is the Python interface to CHASE. It is installed with pip install chase-cps (see Installation ). Its modules are grouped as follows: Contract algebra ( chase_cps.contract ): the class Contract , with the methods compose , conjoin , disjoin , merge , divide , separate , imply , coimply , invert , assume , ensure , saturate , and simplify . Contract-based verification ( chase_cps.checks , chase_cps.models ): refines , verify , is_compatible , is_consistent , is_implementation , is_environment , is_receptive , and remove_redundant ; the class Model , for state machines. Queries on formulas ( chase_cps.logic ): implies , is_satisfiable , and unsat_core . GR(1) synthesis ( chase_cps.gr1 ): is_realizable , synthesize , unrealizable_core , is_well_separated , is_vacuous , and remove_redundant(c, synth=True) . Repair and optimization ( chase_cps.repair , chase_cps.optimize ): repair , minimize , maximize ( Repair , SMT and optimization ). Continuous time ( chase_cps.sampled ): sampled , the stricter formula to check at the samples ( sampled signals ). All the names are also in chase_cps itself. The contracts are read and written in other formats with: load_spec(path) , parse_spec(text) : read the contracts of a specification file ; to_spec(contracts) writes one. parse_sva(text) : reads SystemVerilog Assertions as a contract; to_sva(contract) writes a contract as a checker module (see SystemVerilog Assertions ). to_gr1(contract, format=...) : writes a GR(1) contract for slugs or gr1c (see GR(1) synthesis ). load_dsl(path) : reads a problem written in the domain-specific language of CHASE. load_smv(path) and load_c(path) : read an SMV model with its specifications, and the functions of a C file with their clauses, as contracts with their implementations ( Model checking , C programs ). chase_cps.viz draws contracts, components, and systems (see Diagrams ). Formulas # The Python package, the command line (JSON files), and the MCP server read formulas in the standard LTL syntax, over Boolean, integer, real, and word variables. The operators, the types, and the precedence are in Formulas . A contract is built from strings or from a dictionary (the JSON format of the command line and of the MCP server): from chase_cps import Contract c = Contract.from_strings(inputs=["req"], outputs=["grant"], assumptions=["G F !req"], guarantees=["G (req -> F grant)"], name="Spec") d = Contract.from_dict({"name": "Spec", "inputs": {"req": "bool", "n": [0, 3], "v": "real"}, "outputs": {"grant": "bool"}, "assumptions": ["G F !req"], "guarantees": ["G (req -> F grant)"]}) Results # Every check returns a result with a status ( valid , invalid , sat , unsat , realizable , unrealizable , or unknown with a reason ), the trace of a failed check, and to_dict() for JSON. The details are in Checks . The full API is in the docstrings: help(chase_cps.refines) , help(chase_cps.repair) , and so on, and in the API reference made from them.

docs.text: Tool integrations # CHASE computes the contract algebra itself, and gives the other questions on contracts to external tools. Each integration writes the contracts as the input of a tool, and reads its answer back: Model checking , with nuXmv or NuSMV: the verification tasks (refinement, compatibility, consistency, implementations, environments), with counterexamples and cores. GR(1) synthesis , with slugs or gr1c: whether a component can be synthesized from a contract in the GR(1) fragment, the controllers, and the explanation of an unrealizable contract. C programs , with ESBMC or CBMC: C functions checked against contracts, written in Python or in the clauses of the C file. Hardware: SVA and RTL , with any tool that reads SVA (Jasper, simulators) and with Yosys: contracts read from SystemVerilog Assertions and written back as checker modules, and RTL read as state machines and checked against contracts. SMT and optimization , with z3: the formulas over a bounded number of steps (static contracts, signal temporal logic), and the optimization problems of CHASE (best values, worst cases, repair), which are the problems of a MILP. How to install each tool is on the Installation page.

docs.text: C programs # A C function is a component that answers once: its parameters are the inputs of the contract, by name, and its return value is the output; a pointer parameter named as an output is written by the function. The formulas of such a contract have no temporal operator. is_implementation takes a CFunction and checks it with ESBMC or, without it, CBMC ( chase-cps install esbmc on Linux, brew install esbmc on macOS): from chase_cps import CFunction, Contract, is_implementation open("saturate.c", "w").write(""" int saturate(int x, int lo, int hi) { if (x < lo) return lo; if (x > hi) return hi; return x; } """) sat = Contract.from_strings(name="Sat", inputs={"x": (-1000, 1000), "lo": (-100, 100), "hi": (-100, 100)}, outputs={"y": (-1000, 1000)}, assumptions=["lo <= hi"], guarantees=["y >= lo & y <= hi", "(x >= lo & x <= hi) -> y = x"]) r = is_implementation(CFunction("saturate.c", "saturate"), sat) print(r.status, r.backend) # valid esbmc The checker calls the function with any values of the inputs, within their types and the assumptions, and checks the guarantees on what it returns. A failure gives the values of a call that breaks them (the trace). The checkers also check the function itself: an arithmetic overflow, a division by zero, or an access out of bounds makes the result invalid, with the property in the reason . Loops are unwound up to unwind times (20, is_implementation(f, c, unwind=100) ); a loop that needs more makes the result unknown. Integers are compared as integers (in long long ); a real variable is a double or a float of the function, and its formulas are computed in double , with rounding. Words are not written in C yet. On the command line: chase-cps check spec.ltl --impl saturate.c:saturate Sat . A function called once per step (a controller) implements a contract over steps too. The contract has no assumption, and each guarantee is a formula of one step phi at some steps: phi , X phi , G phi , or G[a,b] phi . Each step of the system is a call on inputs that nothing constrains, so the function implements the contract exactly when each call satisfies every such phi : the checker checks one call, and a call that breaks one, repeated at every step, is the counterexample. from chase_cps import CFunction, is_implementation, parse_spec open("heater.c", "w").write(""" int thermostat(int T) { if (T < 74) return 3; return 0; } """) c = parse_spec("""NAME: t; CONTRACT Thermostat: input integer (0:200) variable T; output integer (0:3) variable u; Assumptions: true; Guarantees: G[0,9] ((T < 74 -> u = 3) & (T >= 74 -> u = 0)); """) is_implementation(CFunction("heater.c", "thermostat"), c["Thermostat"]).status # valid The result is unknown, with the reason, for a function that keeps a state between calls (a static variable, or a global variable of its file that it uses), and for a contract that does not have this form ( T' = T + u - 1 relates two steps). The contract can be written in the C file, next to the code, in the clauses of ESBMC ( __ESBMC_requires(...) , __ESBMC_ensures(...) in the body, __ESBMC_return_value ) or of CBMC ( __CPROVER_requires(...) , __CPROVER_ensures(...) between the signature and the body, __CPROVER_return_value ), or in ACSL, the language of Frama-C (a comment /*@ requires ...; ensures ...; */ just before the function, with \result , ==> , <==> , and chains such as 0 <= T <= 200 ; \old , \at , the quantifiers, and behaviors are not read). load_c (it gives {name: (contract, function)} ) reads each function of the file as a contract and the function as its implementation: the requires clauses are the assumptions, the ensures clauses the guarantees, the parameters the inputs, the return value the output FUNCTION_out , and *p the output p of a pointer parameter. The ranges of the inputs are those of their C types, narrowed by the bounds the requires clauses give: from chase_cps import is_implementation, load_c open("thermostat.c", "w").write(""" int thermostat(int T) { __ESBMC_requires(T >= 0 && T <= 200); __ESBMC_ensures(T >= 74 || __ESBMC_return_value == 3); __ESBMC_ensures(T < 74 || __ESBMC_return_value == 0); return T < 74 ? 3 : 0; } """) c, f = load_c("thermostat.c")["thermostat"] print(c.inputs, is_implementation(f, c).status) # {'T': (0, 200)} valid The clauses are expressions of C over numbers and Booleans ( && || ! == != < <= > >= + - * / ); a conditional ( a ? b : c ) is not read. The clauses on pointers ( is_fresh , r_ok , w_ok , rw_ok , assigns ) are not part of the contract. The function is checked with the clauses taken out of the code, so either checker checks a file with the clauses of the other. A function with no clause has a contract with no term: its check is that of the code alone (overflow, division by zero, access out of bounds, failed assert). chase-cps view FILE.c draws each function as a component with its code, checked: the tag M ⊨ C for a function with clauses, and safe for one with none. A failure shows the call that breaks it, and the term it breaks in red.

docs.text: Model checking # The contract-based verification tasks reduce to the validity or the satisfiability of LTL formulas, which a model checker decides: nuXmv : LTL over Boolean, integer, real, and word variables. Free for academic and non-commercial use. NuSMV : the same without real variables, used when nuXmv is not installed. Both are installed with chase-cps install ( Installation ). With backend="auto" (the default) CHASE takes nuXmv when it is installed, and NuSMV otherwise; the formulas over a bounded number of steps go to z3 when it is installed ( SMT and optimization ). A failed check comes with a counterexample, read back from the trace of the model checker. Engines of nuXmv # nuXmv checks the formulas with IC3 and BDDs at the same time, and the first verdict is taken. Both engines prove and refute, so the verdict does not depend on which one answers; the counterexample may. One engine can be chosen with engine , or in the back end, as the results name it: portfolio (the default): IC3 and BDDs at the same time. ic3 : proves and refutes; good for large state spaces, words, and reals. bdd : proves and refutes; good when a counterexample needs a long loop (a counter that goes around). bmc : finds counterexamples up to bmc_bound steps, and proves nothing; good for short counterexamples. from chase_cps import implies r = implies("cnt = 254 & G (cnt' = cnt + 1)", "X (cnt = 0)", {"cnt": "word[8]"}, "nuxmv/bdd") print(r.status, r.backend) # invalid nuxmv/bdd On the command line the option is --engine . Formulas with signed() or unsigned() are checked with BDDs only: in our tests, IC3 of nuXmv 2.2.0 did not give the same answers as BDDs on them. docs.text: SMT and optimization (z3) # This page is for readers whose contracts compare numbers: budgets, sizings, timing bounds, signals over a bounded horizon. CHASE gives such questions, and every optimization, to the SMT solver z3 , installed with the package: $> pip install "chase-cps[z3]" Checks of formulas over a bounded number of steps # A formula with no G , F , U , or R reads a bounded number of steps: X , x' , past(x, n) , and intervals such as G[0,10] p or F[1,3] p . A contract made of such formulas is a static contract (one step) or a contract of signal temporal logic in discrete time. Its checks are questions of arithmetic over the values of the variables at each step, which z3 answers exactly for linear arithmetic over integers and reals, with any Boolean structure. With z3 installed, CHASE sends these formulas to z3 by itself, in every check of contract-based verification , and the result names the back end z3 . Formulas with G , F , U , or R over the whole behavior go to the model checker , and so do words (bit vectors). Optimization: the problems of a MILP # The optimization questions of CHASE are linear problems over integers, reals, and Boolean structure, the problems that a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) solves: minimize and maximize : the best value of a term where the constraints of a contract hold, and the values that reach it ( formulas over a bounded number of steps ); the worst case of a formula under constraints, its robustness , as for the latency bounds of ContrACT in the Drone timing demo; the values of named constants at the least cost, in repair . z3 solves them with its optimization engine (νZ: Bjørner, Phan, and Fleckenstein, TACAS 2015). It computes with rational numbers, so the optimum is exact and a strict inequality is kept as it is (an optimum that is not reached is reported as such); a disjunction or an implication is written as it is, with no big-M constant; and the variables need no bounds. Each optimum is checked again by the solver before it is given. Dedicated MILP solvers (SCIP, HiGHS) are planned for problems with thousands of variables, with z3 checking their answers. Running another solver # chase-cps export FILE --to smt writes a check as SMT-LIB 2, for z3, cvc5, or another solver you run yourself ( command line ). When the checks run with NuSMV, which has no real type, z3 also refines the abstraction of the comparisons of reals ( real variables ). The demos Drone climb , Room thermostat , and Drone timing are checked and optimized by z3.

docs.text: GR(1) synthesis # The algebra and the verification tasks hold for any contracts. This page is about contracts in the GR(1) fragment of LTL, for which a component can be synthesized. The analyses ask whether a component can be synthesized from a contract: a controller that sets the outputs so that the guarantees hold against every environment that sets the inputs and meets the assumptions. This depends on the synthesis approach, here GR(1) with slugs ; it is not a property of contracts in general. The examples below are from the Charger demo : two robots ask for a charging station ( req1 , req2 ), and an arbiter gives it ( grant1 , grant2 ). The GR(1) form # Each assumption and guarantee must be one of: Kind Form Example initial no temporal operator !grant1 safety G f , with only X (or x' ) in f G !(grant1 & grant2) justice G F f G F req1 In addition, the environment cannot read the next value of the outputs: the initial assumptions read the inputs only, and the safety assumptions read only the next value of the inputs. A contract that is not in this form gives unknown , with the term at fault. Realizability and synthesis # Python Answer is_realizable(c) realizable , or unrealizable with the counter-strategy of the environment synthesize(c) the same, and the controller (a state machine) when realizable Example. The arbiter Greedy gives the station to a robot at the next step after its request, and never to both: G (req1 -> X grant1) R6.1 G (req2 -> X grant2) R6.2 G !(grant1 & grant2) R5 When both robots ask at once, it cannot keep its promise: Greedy is unrealizable. The arbiter Fair promises a grant eventually instead, G F (grant1 | !req1) , and is realizable: cs = load_spec("Charger/charger.ltl") is_realizable(cs["Greedy"]).status # unrealizable r = synthesize(cs["Fair"]) # realizable, a controller with 18 states Writing the specification for a GR(1) solver # slugs is the solver that CHASE runs. To run a solver yourself, to_gr1(c, format=...) writes the contract as its input: format="slugs" (the default): the file that chase-cps gives to slugs. format="gr1c" : the input of gr1c . open("fair.structuredSlugs", "w").write(to_gr1(cs["Fair"])) open("fair.spc", "w").write(to_gr1(cs["Fair"], format="gr1c")) # gr1c -r fair.spc realizability The inputs of the contract are the variables of the environment, and its outputs are those of the system. gr1c compares an integer only with a constant. Thus, for gr1c, a relation with arithmetic or between variables ( x' = x + 1 ) is written as the values that satisfy it. Unrealizable cores # An unrealizable contract can have many guarantees. unrealizable_core (or is_realizable(c, core=True) ) gives a minimal set of guarantees that is unrealizable under all the assumptions: remove any one, and the rest is realizable. r = is_realizable(cs["Greedy"], core=True) r.core.core.guarantees G (req1 -> X grant1) G (req2 -> X grant2) G !(grant1 & grant2) The two initial guarantees of Greedy ( !grant1 , !grant2 ) are not in the core: they play no part in the conflict. The search follows QuickCore (Maoz and Shalom, ICSE 2021). Well-separation # A contract is realizable for a bad reason when the controller can win by making the environment break its assumptions. Such a controller satisfies the contract (A → G holds when A fails) without doing its job. Example. The arbiter Pushy assumes two things about robot 1: G F req1 A2 robot 1 asks infinitely often G (grant1 -> X !req1) A3 robot 1 stops asking after a grant If the arbiter gives grant1 at every step, A3 makes robot 1 stop asking from the next step on, and A2 can then never hold. The arbiter wins without serving anybody. is_well_separated finds it: r = is_well_separated(cs["Pushy"], core=True) r.status # not_separated r.core.core.assumptions # A2 and A3 r.controller # the strategy that forces the violation is_well_separated(cs["Polite"]).status # separated Polite assumes G ((req1 & grant1) -> X !req1) instead of A3: robot 1 stops asking only after a grant it asked for. The arbiter can no longer force a violation, and the contract is well-separated. The check asks whether the controller can still win with the goal G F false (Klein and Pnueli, HVC 2010; Maoz and Ringert, FSE 2016): if it can, it wins only by breaking the assumptions, while keeping its own initial and safety guarantees. Vacuity # A contract is vacuous when the controller can win without an output that a liveness guarantee asks for: the assumptions already make the guarantee hold, and it obliges nothing. is_vacuous strengthens the guarantees and asks slugs whether the contract is still realizable (Bloem, Chockler, Ebrahimi, and Strichman, FMSD 2021): Mode Query, for an output y Meaning never A, G + a winning strategy never sets y eventually A, G + {!p, G (p → X p), G (p → !y), G F p}, p a new output a winning strategy stops setting y from some step on The outputs checked are those that a justice guarantee asks to set (they occur only positively in it). Example. Fair is not vacuous: it cannot win without granting each robot. An arbiter that trusts the robots to stop asking on their own is: fair = cs["Fair"] trusting = Contract("Trusting", fair.inputs, fair.outputs, [ltl.parse("G F !req1"), ltl.parse("G F !req2")], fair.guarantees) is_vacuous(fair).status # not_vacuous r = is_vacuous(trusting, core=True) for v in r.vacuous: print(v.output, v.mode, [ltl.to_str(a) for a in v.core.core]) grant1 never ['G F !req1'] grant2 never ['G F !req2'] With G F !req1, the guarantee G F (grant1 | !req1) holds without any grant. The core is the assumption that makes it so; it is too strong. Redundancy in the GR(1) game # A term is redundant in the game when removing it does not change the synthesis problem: the same contracts are realizable, with the same controllers (the inherent vacuity of Maoz and Shalom, ESEC/FSE 2020). remove_redundant(c, synth=True) removes these terms. Example. Fair has these justice guarantees: G F (grant1 | !req1) R7.1 G F (grant2 | !req2) R7.2 G F (grant1 | !req1 | grant2) R8 R8 is weaker than R7.1, so it adds nothing: v = remove_redundant(cs["Fair"], synth=True, core=True) for t in v.removed: print(t.part, t.kind, ltl.to_str(t.term), [ltl.to_str(x) for x in t.core]) guarantee justice G F (grant1 | !req1 | grant2) ['G F (grant1 | !req1)'] Without synth , remove_redundant ( contract-based verification ) keeps A → G instead. The two differ only when the assumptions are wrong: in the game, the component must keep its safety guarantees even when the environment breaks its justice assumptions. Use synth=True before synthesis, and the default before the algebra and the checks.

docs.text: Hardware: SVA and RTL # This page is for hardware designers: contracts written in SystemVerilog Assertions, checked against RTL, and written back as checker modules for a formal tool or a simulator. parse_sva reads the assume property and assert property statements of SystemVerilog as a contract: the assumptions and the guarantees. The text can be a module, a bind file, or the statements alone. to_sva writes a contract as a checker module, which any tool that reads SVA can check, formal or simulator. Nothing in either is specific to a tool. In the MCP server the tools have the same names. from chase_cps import ltl, parse_sva r = parse_sva(""" module arbiter (input logic clk, input logic rst, input logic req, output logic gnt, output logic [7:0] count); default clocking @(posedge clk); endclocking default disable iff (rst); A0: assume property (req |=> !req); G0: assert property (req |-> ##[1:2] gnt); G1: assert property (gnt |=> count == $past(count) + 1); endmodule""") print(r.contract.inputs, r.contract.outputs) for p in r.properties: print(p.label, ltl.to_str(p.formula)) print(r.skipped) # the statements not read, with the reason Reading # SVA Contract assert property (p) the guarantee G p : an assertion is checked at every cycle assume property (p) , restrict property (p) the assumption G p initial assert property (p) p , at the first cycle cover property (p) kept apart, in covers logic [7:0] x , logic signed [7:0] x word[8] , signed word[8] ; a 1-bit signal is a Boolean logic [3:0][7:0] x word[32] ; x[2] is bits 23 to 16 u1.state u1__state , mapped back in names One step of LTL is one cycle of the clock. The widths are those of Verilog: the operands of an operation are extended to the width of the context first, so in count == $past(count) + 1 the sum has 32 bits (as the constant 1) and does not wrap around; the property fails when count goes from 255 to 0. What is read: The property operators: not , and , or , implies , iff , |-> , |=> , #-# , #=# , if / else , nexttime , always , s_always , eventually , s_eventually , until , s_until , until_with , s_until_with , strong , weak . The sequences of bounded length: ##n , ##[m:n] , [*m:n] , and , or , intersect , throughout , within , first_match . ##[m:$] is read in an antecedent and in a strong sequence. The system functions $past , $rose , $fell , $stable , $changed , $onehot , $onehot0 , $countones . disable iff , default clocking , and default disable iff . Named properties and sequences, with arguments. assign and wire x = e . A property that looks before the first cycle is checked from the cycle where the past exists ( from_cycle ): x == $past(x) from cycle 1. Values two cycles apart or more are written with past(x, n) . In a consequent, a |-> ##[1:$] b is weak in an assert and never fails, so it is not read: write a |-> s_eventually b . A contract has one clock: with several, clock chooses one (by default the clock of most properties), and the properties of the other clocks are skipped. The directions come from inputs or outputs , then from the ports of the module. Signals without a declaration are read as 1-bit signals and listed in undeclared . What is not read, and listed in skipped with the reason: local variables; [->n] and [=n] , and unbounded repetition; unpacked arrays; the digits x and z ; immediate assertions. Writing # from chase_cps import Contract, to_sva c = Contract.from_dict({"name": "Arb", "inputs": {"req": "bool"}, "outputs": {"gnt": "bool", "count": "word[8]"}, "assumptions": ["G (req -> X !req)"], "guarantees": ["G (req -> X gnt | X X gnt)", "G (gnt -> count' = count + 1)"]}) print(to_sva(c, reset="rst", bind="arbiter")) A formula G p is checked at every cycle. Any other formula is checked once, at the first cycle ( initial ). The variables are written as follows: a word is a vector; an integer range is an int , with its range assumed (an input) or asserted (an output); a real variable cannot be written. The options of to_sva : reset : the properties are disabled while it holds. bind : adds a bind statement that puts the checker in a design module, with its ports connected by name. The attribute (* chase = "output" *) keeps the role of each signal for parse_sva ; the tools ignore it. Meaning # The meaning is that of the standard, IEEE 1800-2017 (chapter 16, and Annex F for disable iff ), not that of a tool. Tools may differ in corner cases: when the failure of an attempt is already decided by the values before a reset, but a sequence of the attempt is still running when the reset comes, the standard gives a failure and some tools a disabled attempt. To compare with a tool, run its checks on the SVA. RTL # A Verilog or SystemVerilog module is a state machine: Model.from_rtl(files, top) reads it with Yosys ( pip install chase-cps[rtl] ), and is_implementation , is_environment , and is_receptive take it. The ports are the variables of the contracts (a 1-bit port is a Boolean, a wider one a word), and one step is one cycle. from chase_cps import Model, is_implementation m = Model.from_rtl(["bsg_dff_reset.sv", "bsg_dff_en.sv", "bsg_one_fifo.sv"], "bsg_one_fifo", parameters={"width_p": 4}, reset="reset_i", names={"ready_and_o": "ready_o"}) print(is_implementation(m, slot).status) parameters sets the parameters of the top module, names renames ports, defines gives macros, and reset holds the reset in the first step and checks the contracts from the step after it. The checks are those of nuXmv, for small and medium designs. The Buffer swap demo checks the RTL of two FIFOs.

In the MCP server the tools have the same names. from chase_cps import ltl, parse_sva r = parse_sva(""" module arbiter (input logic clk, input logic rst, input logic req, output logic gnt, output logic [7:0] count); default clocking @(posedge clk); endclocking default disable iff (rst); A0: assume property (req |=> !req); G0: assert property (req |-> ##[1:2] gnt); G1: assert property (gnt |=> count == $past(count) + 1); endmodule""") print(r.contract.inputs, r.contract.outputs) for p in r.properties: print(p.label, ltl.to_str(p.formula)) print(r.skipped) # the statements not read, with the reason

The widths are those of Verilog: the operands of an operation are extended to the width of the context first, so in count == $past(count) + 1 the sum has 32 bits (as the constant 1) and does not wrap around; the property fails when count goes from 255 to 0. What is read: The property operators: not , and , or , implies , iff , |-> , |=> , #-# , #=# , if / else , nexttime , always , s_always , eventually , s_eventually , until , s_until , until_with , s_until_with , strong , weak . The sequences of bounded length: ##n , ##[m:n] , [*m:n] , and , or , intersect , throughout , within , first_match . ##[m:$] is read in an antecedent and in a strong sequence. The system functions $past , $rose , $fell , $stable , $changed , $onehot , $onehot0 , $countones . disable iff , default clocking , and default disable iff . Named properties and sequences, with arguments. assign and wire x = e . A property that looks before the first cycle is checked from the cycle where the past exists ( from_cycle ): x == $past(x) from cycle 1. Values two cycles apart or more are written with past(x, n) . In a consequent, a |-> ##[1:$] b is weak in an assert and never fails, so it is not read: write a |-> s_eventually b . A contract has one clock: with several, clock chooses one (by default the clock of most properties), and the properties of the other clocks are skipped. The directions come from inputs or outputs , then from the ports of the module. Signals without a declaration are read as 1-bit signals and listed in undeclared . What is not read, and listed in skipped with the reason: local variables; [->n] and [=n] , and unbounded repetition; unpacked arrays; the digits x and z ; immediate assertions.

docs.text: from chase_cps import Contract, to_sva c = Contract.from_dict({"name": "Arb", "inputs": {"req": "bool"}, "outputs": {"gnt": "bool", "count": "word[8]"}, "assumptions": ["G (req -> X !req)"], "guarantees": ["G (req -> X gnt | X X gnt)", "G (gnt -> count' = count + 1)"]}) print(to_sva(c, reset="rst", bind="arbiter")) A formula G p is checked at every cycle. Any other formula is checked once, at the first cycle ( initial ). The variables are written as follows: a word is a vector; an integer range is an int , with its range assumed (an input) or asserted (an output); a real variable cannot be written. The options of to_sva : reset : the properties are disabled while it holds. bind : adds a bind statement that puts the checker in a design module, with its ports connected by name. The attribute (* chase = "output" *) keeps the role of each signal for parse_sva ; the tools ignore it.

docs.text: The meaning is that of the standard, IEEE 1800-2017 (chapter 16, and Annex F for disable iff ), not that of a tool. Tools may differ in corner cases: when the failure of an attempt is already decided by the values before a reset, but a sequence of the attempt is still running when the reset comes, the standard gives a failure and some tools a disabled attempt. To compare with a tool, run its checks on the SVA.

docs.text: A Verilog or SystemVerilog module is a state machine: Model.from_rtl(files, top) reads it with Yosys ( pip install chase-cps[rtl] ), and is_implementation , is_environment , and is_receptive take it. The ports are the variables of the contracts (a 1-bit port is a Boolean, a wider one a word), and one step is one cycle. from chase_cps import Model, is_implementation m = Model.from_rtl(["bsg_dff_reset.sv", "bsg_dff_en.sv", "bsg_one_fifo.sv"], "bsg_one_fifo", parameters={"width_p": 4}, reset="reset_i", names={"ready_and_o": "ready_o"}) print(is_implementation(m, slot).status) parameters sets the parameters of the top module, names renames ports, defines gives macros, and reset holds the reset in the first step and checks the contracts from the step after it. The checks are those of nuXmv, for small and medium designs. The Buffer swap demo checks the RTL of two FIFOs.
